docs.title: HQL
docs.text:
HQL, the Hyper Query Language, is a statically typed expression and query language. It combines functional expressions with pipelines over files, streams, structured data and HyperMarkDown documents, and checks a program's types before it evaluates it.

type Book { title : String, year : Int, rating : Int }

books = [
    Book(title = "Dune", year = 1965, rating = 5),
    Book(title = "Emma", year = 1815, rating = 3),
    Book(title = "Beloved", year = 1987, rating = 4),
]

books
| filter(b => b.rating >= 4)
| sort(b => b.title)
| map(b => b.title)

["Beloved", "Dune"]

source reads the documents a file holds, and target writes a value to one:

source(file("sightings.jsonl"), Json)
| filter(s => s.seen == "morning")
| target(file("morning.json"))
  • Install — a release binary or cargo install hql.
  • Learn HQL — the book, one runnable program at a time.
  • Reference — the grammar, the command line, and reporting.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The example corpus is where HQL's features are designed: an example is written first, and the implementation is held to it. Each query file declares its expected type and result in a header, and the test suite runs every one.

Corpus What it shows tutorial The reading-club vault the HQL book runs against: books, authors, their links and a relation card notebook A document whose cells share values by id, built with hql render birds Linked cards with runnable collection queries: repeated sightings, distinct species, keyed counts, ordered routes and sorted keys — plus intentional errors for duplicate keys and non-orderable sorted-map keys mapreduce Book cards filtered, grouped and reduced, read as a chain of steps functions Declared, generic and aliased functions, partial application, and intentional errors streams Generators with yield, an unbounded stream ended by take, and the lazy steps

docs.title: Reading a query header
docs.text:
// status: valid-now
// feature: Bird cards filtered and sorted by name
// implementation: implemented
// vault: birds/wiki
// expected-type: Seq<String>
// expected: ["Barn owl", "Common raven", "European robin"]

A header may instead say status: proposed with implementation: pending and a proposal: naming the record that specifies it. Such a case is a design input, pinned before it runs, and the suite asserts that it does not check yet — the day it does, it has to be promoted.

docs.title: Running one
docs.text:
From a clone, after cargo build --locked:

target/debug/hql --vault examples/birds/wiki run examples/birds/queries/catalog.hql

docs.title: From a release
docs.text:
Each release ships a binary for every supported target, with a checksum beside it. Download the pair from the releases page, check it, and put hql somewhere on your PATH:

shasum -a 256 -c hql-<version>-<target>.tar.gz.sha256   # sha256sum -c on Linux
tar -xzf hql-<version>-<target>.tar.gz

The targets are x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-apple-darwin and x86_64-apple-darwin. Verify the archive against the published SHA-256 checksum before extracting it.

docs.title: With Cargo
docs.text:
With Rust 1.95 or newer from rustup:

cargo install hql --locked                                   # the last release
cargo install --git https://github.com/ewiger/hql --locked   # the latest commit
cargo install --path . --locked                              # from a clone

docs.title: Check it works
docs.text:
hql eval '40 + 2'

42

hql builtins lists every step a pipeline may use, grouped by the extension that provides it.

Versions

While the major version is 0, a minor release may change the language incompatibly. The changelog lists each such change by release.

docs.title: Learn HQL
docs.text:
This is a book about HQL, read from the first page to the last. It starts with a number and ends with an agent whose run is a value, and every chapter builds on the ones before it. Every program in it prints what the book shows. Chapters 1 to 12 run with the current release; chapters 13 to 15 cover the io, io.logging and ai modules, which ship in the next one.

HQL is a statically typed language for querying, transforming, connecting and computing over data, knowledge and AI workflows. A program is checked before it runs, and values flow through pipelines of typed steps: over records and lists, as jq works over JSON; over tables, as SQL does; over files, standard input and streams that do not end; over a vault of Markdown documents, their links and their meaning; and through the context, prompts and runs of a language model.

docs.title: Following along
docs.text:
Install hql, clone the repository for the tutorial vault, and run each program with hql eval:

git clone https://github.com/ewiger/hql && cd hql
hql --vault examples/tutorial eval 'cards | size'

The tutorial vault, examples/tutorial/, is a small reading club: seven books, five authors, the links between them, and one claim about which book inspired which.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text:
1. Hello world — the first program, running it, and the check before a program runs.
  2. Data types — Int, Float, String and Bool in the REPL, Data and its JSON-shaped trees, Option for a value that may be missing, and how sets, Data and maps differ.
  3. Collections — lists, sets and maps, and the steps they share.
  4. Functions — lambdas, declared and generic functions, aliases, and partial application.
  5. SQL-like Queries — where, order by, group by and the aggregates.
  6. A vault of documents — cards, their metadata, and a reading list nobody maintains.
  7. Links and graphs — following links, building graphs, drawing them.
  8. Finding cards by meaning — rankings, hits, and the evidence behind a score.
  9. Streams that do not end — generators, laziness, and batches.
  10. Writing results out — presentation formats and who chooses them.
  11. Queries inside documents — cells, and documents built from them.
  12. Working with hql — the commands, the reports, and what to do when something is wrong.
  13. Reading and writing data — endpoints, source, tap, target and sink, and hql as a command-line data tool.
  14. Channels and logs — values passed through channels, and structured logging.
  15. Agents and runs — agents as cards, context and prompts, tools, and runs kept as values.
  16. Types, traits and modules — records, unions, results, receiver calls, traits and operators, and modules of your own.

docs.title: 1. Hello world
docs.text: HQL is a statically typed expression and query language. A program is an expression, or a few statements ending in one; hql checks its type, then evaluates it, and writes the value. This chapter is about that loop.

docs.title: Hello, world
docs.text:
The smallest program that says hello is the text itself:

"Hello, world!"

"Hello, world!"

A program is an expression, and its value is what hql writes. fmt writes values into a template, one {} each:

fmt("Hello, {}!", "world")

"Hello, world!"

docs.title: Running a program
docs.text:
hql eval takes a program as an argument:

hql eval '"Hello, world!"'

Every program in this book runs that way. Most of them run against the tutorial vault, a small reading club in examples/tutorial/, so the commands in later chapters start with hql --vault examples/tutorial eval. The book shows each program in an hql block and what hql writes in the block after it.

1 + 2

3

docs.title: Values and their types
docs.text:
Every value has a type: 1 + 2 is an Int, "Hello" a String. hql check writes a program's type without evaluating it:

$ hql check - <<< '7 / 2'
Int

Chapter 2 meets the types one by one.

docs.title: Checked before it runs
docs.text:
A program is checked as a whole before anything is evaluated. A type error names the expression it found and points at it:

1 + "two"

type error: addition requires two Int, two Float or two Decimal operands
 --> <expression>:1:5
  |
1 | 1 + "two"
  |     ^^^^^

Nothing ran: there is no value, only the report, and the exit status is 1. The same holds for a name nobody bound:

pages + 1

name error: `pages` is not bound
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | pages + 1
  | ^^^^^

docs.title: Bindings
docs.text:
name = expression binds a value to a name for the statements after it. The program's value is its last expression.

pages = 280
chapters = 24
pages / chapters

11

A binding may state its type, and the checker holds the value to it:

rating : Int = 5
rating

5

docs.title: Choosing a value
docs.text:
a given condition otherwise b is a when the condition holds, and b otherwise. It is an expression, so it has a type: both branches have one.

pages = 412
"long" given pages > 300 otherwise "short"

"long"

match compares one value against patterns, in order, and the first that fits gives the result:

status = "reading"
match status {
    "done" => "finished",
    "reading" => "on the nightstand",
    _ => "on the shelf",
}

"on the nightstand"

A match that does not cover every case is refused before it runs; _ is the pattern that fits anything.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 2 meets the data types: Int, Float, String and Bool, tried in the REPL, and Data, the records and lists that JSON and YAML are made of.

docs.title: 3. Collections
docs.text: A Data list holds trees. Most collections in HQL hold values of one known type, and say what they promise about order and repetition. This chapter meets them, and the steps every collection shares.

docs.title: Lists, sets and maps
docs.text:
A list keeps every element at its position, duplicates included:

[412, 280, 310, 145]

[412, 280, 310, 145]

A set keeps each distinct value once and promises no order. Braces around values, rather than fields, write one:

{"novel", "essay", "novel", "poetry"}

{"novel", "essay", "poetry"}

A value prints as the literal that writes it, so a set prints in braces and a string inside a collection keeps its quotes. hql check writes a program's type without running it:

{"novel", "essay", "novel", "poetry"}

Set<String>

A map pairs each key with one value. Map(keys, values) builds one, and get looks a key up — an Option, since the key may be missing:

pages = Map(["Dune", "Frankenstein"], [412, 280])
get(pages, "Dune")

412

docs.title: A step keeps its input's shape
docs.text:
Steps work on any collection, and each returns the kind of collection it was given wherever it can: a list stays a list, a set stays a set.

[412, 280, 310, 145] | sort | take(2)

[145, 280]

[412, 280, 310, 145] | drop(1)

[280, 310, 145]

A set has no order of its own, so sort gives it one and the result is a list. And because a set keeps each value once, mapping it can make it smaller:

{3, 1, 2} | map(n => n * 0)

{0}

[3, 1, 2] | map(n => n * 0)

[0, 0, 0]

size, count and contains ask about a whole collection:

genres = ["novel", "essay", "novel"]
[genres | size, genres | count("novel")]

[3, 2]

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
sort orders by a value's own order. sort(by = key) orders by a key, and a function of two values that returns an Ordering orders by comparison:

[412, 280, 310] | sort((a, b) => compare(b, a))

[412, 310, 280]

min and max find the least and greatest value. Over an empty list there is none, and the type says so: the result is an Option.

[412, 280, 310] | min

280

[] | List<Int> | min

none

[] | List<Int> is a constructor written as a step: x | T is T(x). A constructor builds a value of its type — Set(xs), List(xs), Map(keys, values) — and the pipeline form reads left to right:

["novel", "essay", "novel", "poetry"] | Set | size

3

docs.title: Positions are promises
docs.text:
A list, a ranking and a sequence of cards have positions; a set does not. A step that needs positions refuses a set, and says what to write instead:

{3, 1, 2} | drop(1)

type error: `drop` needs values in a stable order, and Set<Int> has none; sort it first
 --> <expression>:1:13
  |
1 | {3, 1, 2} | drop(1)
  |             ^^^^^^^

The checker knows each collection's promises from its type, so this is found before anything runs, not after a wrong answer.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Steps take functions — n => n * 0, (a, b) => compare(b, a). Chapter 4 is about functions themselves: naming them, passing them, and making them generic.

docs.title: 4. Functions
docs.text: A function is a value like any other. It can be bound to a name, passed to a step, returned from another function, and written once for every type it works on.

docs.title: Lambdas and their types
docs.text:
n => n * 2 is a lambda. Written as an argument, it takes its parameter's type from the step it is passed to. Written on its own, it states the type:

double = (n: Int) => n * 2
[412, 280] | map(double)

[824, 560]

A function's type is written with an arrow: Int -> Int, (Int, Int) -> Int.

double = (n: Int) => n * 2
double

Int -> Int

Piping into a function calls it: x | f is f(x).

double = (n: Int) => n * 2
280 | double

560

docs.title: Declared functions
docs.text:
fn declares a function with typed parameters and a result type. Its name is bound before its body is checked, so it may call itself:

fn factorial(n: Int) : Int = 1 given n <= 1 otherwise n * factorial(n - 1)
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5] | map(factorial)

[1, 2, 6, 24, 120]

A function may take a function, and return one. The returned function keeps the values it captured:

fn adder(k: Int) : Int -> Int = n => n + k
fn twice(f: Int -> Int, x: Int) : Int = f(f(x))
twice(adder(3), 30)

36

A last parameter written ...T collects any number of trailing arguments into a list:

fn total(xs: ...Int) : Int = xs | sum
[total(), total(1, 2), total(1, 2, 3, 4)]

[0, 3, 10]

docs.title: Generic functions
docs.text:
A function written once for every type names a type parameter, one capital letter in angle brackets. Each call fills it from its arguments:

fn first<T>(xs: List<T>) : Option<T> = xs | reduce((a, b) => a)
first(["Dune", "Emma"])

"Dune"

The same function over a list of numbers gives an Option<Int>:

fn first<T>(xs: List<T>) : Option<T> = xs | reduce((a, b) => a)
first([412, 280])

Option<Int>

Inside the body T is a type of its own: the body may rely only on what the parameter promises. T : Orderable promises an order, so the body may sort or find a minimum, and each call checks that the promise holds:

fn shortest<T : Orderable>(xs: List<T>) : Option<T> = xs | min
shortest([412, 280, 310])

280

fn shortest<T : Orderable>(xs: List<T>) : Option<T> = xs | min
shortest([{1}, {2}])

type error: `shortest` needs T : Orderable, and T is Set<Int> here
 --> <expression>:2:1
  |
2 | shortest([{1}, {2}])
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
Most small functions are a pipeline fragment with a name. := defines one, and the checker writes its type: the input is the most general one the fragment accepts, and each parameter takes the type of the step argument it fills.

top(n) := sort | take(n)
[412, 280, 310, 145] | top(2)

[145, 280]

hql check prints the signature it wrote:

top(n) := sort | take(n)
1

top : (Collection<T>, Int) -> List<T> where T : Orderable
Int

docs.title: Holes
docs.text:
A call with _ for an argument is a function of the arguments left open — a partial application:

fn add(a: Int, b: Int) : Int = a + b
[1, 2, 3] | map(add(10, _))

[11, 12, 13]

docs.title: Absence, once more
docs.text:
Option<T> is how a function says a value may be missing. some(x) and none build one, match takes one apart, and somes keeps the present values of a collection:

fn rating_of(r: Int) : Option<Int> = some(r) given r > 0 otherwise none
[5, 0, 4] | map(rating_of) | somes

[5, 4]

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: With functions and collections in hand, chapter 5 asks the questions SQL asks: where, order by, group by, and the aggregates.

docs.title: 5. SQL-like Queries
docs.text: SQL asks a table questions: which rows, in what order, how many, grouped by what. HQL asks the same questions with pipeline steps. This chapter works through them over one table — the reading club's shelf, written as a list of records.

docs.title: The table
docs.text:
shelf = [
    {title: "Frankenstein", author: "Mary Shelley", year: 1818, genre: "novel", pages: 280, status: "done", rating: 5},
    {title: "Dune", author: "Frank Herbert", year: 1965, genre: "novel", pages: 412, status: "reading"},
    {title: "The Hobbit", author: "J. R. R. Tolkien", year: 1937, genre: "novel", pages: 310, status: "todo"},
    {title: "Leaves of Grass", author: "Walt Whitman", year: 1855, genre: "poetry", pages: 145, status: "todo"},
    {title: "A Room of One's Own", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1929, genre: "essay", pages: 112, status: "done", rating: 4},
    {title: "The Common Reader", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1925, genre: "essay", pages: 304, status: "todo"},
    {title: "Mrs Dalloway", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1925, genre: "novel", pages: 194, status: "reading"},
]
shelf | size

7

Every program in this chapter begins with these lines; the book shows them once.

docs.title: Select and where
docs.text:
map is SQL's SELECT: it says what to keep of each row. filter is WHERE:

shelf
| filter(b => b.status == "todo")
| map(b => b.title)

["The Hobbit", "Leaves of Grass", "The Common Reader"]

shelf
| filter(b => b.author == "Virginia Woolf")
| map(b => {title: b.title, year: b.year})

[{title: "A Room of One's Own", year: 1929}, {title: "The Common Reader", year: 1925}, {title: "Mrs Dalloway", year: 1925}]

docs.title: Typed views of a record
docs.text:
ORDER BY pages needs pages to be numbers, and a record's leaves have no type of their own. A small function gives a record a typed view — one field, as the type the program means it to be, with what to do when it is missing:

fn title(b: Data) : String = match b.title { some(String t) => t, _ => "" }
fn pages(b: Data) : Int = match b.pages { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }
fn year(b: Data) : Int = match b.year { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }

From here on, the programs begin with the table and these views.

docs.title: Order by and limit
docs.text:
sort(by = key) is ORDER BY, and take(n) is LIMIT. A comparison orders the other way:

shelf
| sort(by = year)
| take(3)
| map(title)

["Frankenstein", "Leaves of Grass", "The Common Reader"]

shelf
| sort((a, b) => compare(pages(b), pages(a)))
| take(2)
| map(b => {title: title(b), pages: pages(b)})

[{pages: 412, title: "Dune"}, {pages: 310, title: "The Hobbit"}]

docs.title: Distinct
docs.text:
A set keeps each value once, so SELECT DISTINCT is the Set constructor:

shelf | map(b => b.genre) | Set

{"novel", "poetry", "essay"}

docs.title: Aggregates
docs.text:
size counts rows. sum, average, min and max work over numbers, so the pages are read through their view first:

lengths = shelf | map(pages)
{books: lengths | size, pages: lengths | sum, longest: lengths | max, average: lengths | average}

{average: 251.0, books: 7, longest: 412, pages: 1757}

Every aggregate is a fold: reduce with a starting value and a way to combine two values. sum is reduce(0, +). max is reduce(max), which starts from the first value and so is an Option: an empty list has none.

lengths = shelf | map(pages)
{total: lengths | reduce(0, +), longest: lengths | reduce(max)}

{longest: 412, total: 1757}

docs.title: Group by
docs.text:
group(by = key) partitions the rows by a key. Each group holds its key and its items, and a map over the groups computes one row per group — SQL's GROUP BY with its aggregates:

shelf
| group(by = b => b.genre)
| map(g => {genre: g.key, books: g.items | size, pages: g.items | map(pages) | sum})

{{books: 4, genre: "novel", pages: 1196}, {books: 1, genre: "poetry", pages: 145}, {books: 2, genre: "essay", pages: 416}}

HAVING is a filter after the group:

shelf
| group(by = b => b.author)
| filter(g => size(g.items) > 1)
| map(g => g.key)

{"Virginia Woolf"}

docs.title: Several answers in one pass
docs.text:
tee names a side branch of a pipeline. The branch reads the same rows, its result is bound to a name, and the main pipeline goes on unchanged. A branch of several steps continues on lines indented past the | before tee:

reading = shelf
| tee unread =
    filter(b => b.status == "todo")
    | size
| tee read =
    filter(b => b.status == "done")
    | size
| filter(b => b.status == "reading")
| map(title)
{unread: unread, read: read, reading: reading}

{read: 2, reading: ["Dune", "Mrs Dalloway"], unread: 3}

docs.title: From SQL to HQL
docs.text:
SQL HQL SELECT title map(b => b.title) WHERE status = 'todo' filter(b => b.status == "todo") ORDER BY year sort(by = year) LIMIT 3 take(3) OFFSET 3 drop(3) SELECT DISTINCT genre map(b => b.genre) \| Set COUNT(*), SUM(pages) size, map(pages) \| sum GROUP BY genre group(by = b => b.genre) HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 filter(g => size(g.items) > 1)

Joins wait for record values of their own, which are on the roadmap.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: The shelf was written by hand. In chapter 6 the same books are documents in a vault, and the same questions are asked of the documents themselves.

docs.title: 6. A vault of documents
docs.text: The shelf of chapter 5 was a list written by hand. Here the same books are documents in a folder, and HQL reads the folder.

docs.title: A vault is a folder
docs.text:
A vault is a directory of Markdown and HyperMarkDown documents. The tutorial vault looks like this:

examples/tutorial/
├── authors/
│   ├── frank-herbert.hmd
│   ├── jrr-tolkien.hmd
│   ├── mary-shelley.hmd
│   ├── virginia-woolf.hmd
│   └── walt-whitman.hmd
├── books/
│   ├── a-room-of-ones-own.hmd
│   ├── dune.hmd
│   ├── frankenstein.hmd
│   ├── leaves-of-grass.hmd
│   ├── mrs-dalloway.hmd
│   ├── the-common-reader.hmd
│   └── the-hobbit.hmd
├── club.hmd
├── frankenstein-inspires-dune.hmd
└── hql.toml

Each document is a card. A card has a header of metadata and a body someone wrote:

---
title: Dune
metadata:
  category: book
  author: Frank Herbert
  year: 1965
  genre: novel
  pages: 412
  status: reading
---
# Dune

A novel by [[frank-herbert]]. A desert planet, a spice, and a family that inherits both.

A program run inside a vault runs against it: hql takes the nearest directory at or above the current one that holds .hmd/ or hql.toml. --vault <directory> names one instead:

hql --vault examples/tutorial eval 'cards | size'

cards | size

14

docs.title: cards
docs.text:
cards is every card of the vault, as a sequence. Its order is the order a sorted walk of the folder reaches each document — the entries of each directory by name, depth first — so a program answers the same on every machine:

cards | take(4) | map(c => c.name)

["frank-herbert", "jrr-tolkien", "mary-shelley", "virginia-woolf"]

A card has the fields of a document: its name (the file stem), title, path, format, body, its kind, and metadata, the header's tree.

docs.title: A link is an optional card
docs.text:
@[[name]] refers to a card by name: @ followed by the link a document writes, [[name]]. A link may point at a document nobody has written yet, so its type is Option<Card>, and reading a field through it reads through the option:

@[[dune]].title

"Dune"

@[[nowhere]].title

none

docs.title: Metadata is Data
docs.text:
A card's metadata is the Data of chapter 2, so every question from chapters 2 and 5 applies. The books are the cards whose category says so:

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
| map(c => c.title)

["A Room of One's Own", "Dune", "Frankenstein", "Leaves of Grass", "Mrs Dalloway", "The Common Reader", "The Hobbit"]

docs.title: The reading list
docs.text:
The club's reading list is the books still to read, by title:

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| sort(by = c => c.title)
| map(c => c.title)

["Leaves of Grass", "The Common Reader", "The Hobbit"]

Read it as three steps, each consuming the one before. filter decides each card on its own; sort needs every card before it can place the first; map turns each card into its title. A step that decides each value alone may run on any part of the input in any order, and a step that needs the whole input is where the parts meet. That is the shape of MapReduce, and HQL keeps it visible in the pipeline: nothing is stored in between, and nothing is a loop.

No one maintains this list. Mark a book status: done in its header and the next run of the query no longer lists it.

docs.title: Grouping cards
docs.text:
group partitions the books by a header value, as it partitioned the shelf:

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
| group(by = c => c.metadata.status)
| map(g => {status: g.key, books: g.items | map(c => c.title)})

{{books: ["A Room of One's Own", "Frankenstein"], status: "done"}, {books: ["Dune", "Mrs Dalloway"], status: "reading"}, {books: ["Leaves of Grass", "The Common Reader", "The Hobbit"], status: "todo"}}

A typed view of a card works as the views of chapter 5 did, and the pages per author are a map over each group and a sum — map, then reduce:

fn pages(c: Card) : Int = match c.metadata.pages { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
| group(by = c => c.metadata.author)
| map(g => {author: g.key, pages: g.items | map(pages) | sum})

{{author: "Virginia Woolf", pages: 610}, {author: "Frank Herbert", pages: 412}, {author: "Mary Shelley", pages: 280}, {author: "Walt Whitman", pages: 145}, {author: "J. R. R. Tolkien", pages: 310}}

docs.title: Kinds of card
docs.text:
A card whose header declares a relation between two other cards is a RelationCard; every other card is a ConceptCard. of_type keeps the cards of one kind:

cards | of_type(RelationCard) | map(c => c.title)

["Frankenstein inspires Dune"]

Chapter 7 is about what that relation means: cards and the links between them form a graph.

docs.title: The vault itself
docs.text:
cards is a binding the standard library makes, cards = vault.cards, over vault, the value the host seeds when it is given a vault:

[vault.name, vault.cards | size | text]

["tutorial", 14]

Outside every vault and without --vault there is no vault, and naming one says so:

cards | size

name error: `cards` needs a vault: run inside one or pass --vault <directory>
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | cards | size
  | ^^^^^

docs.title: 7. Links and graphs
docs.text: A document that writes [[frankenstein]] links to another. The links of a vault make its cards a graph: cards are the nodes, links are the edges. This chapter follows links, builds graphs, and draws them.

docs.title: Following links
docs.text:
An edge goes from the card that wrote the link, its source, to the card it names, its target. uplinks gives the edges leaving a card, and downlinks the edges arriving at it:

@[[mrs-dalloway]] | uplinks

[mrs-dalloway -> virginia-woolf]

@[[virginia-woolf]] | downlinks | map(e => e.source)

["a-room-of-ones-own", "mrs-dalloway", "the-common-reader"]

A link in a body may carry data of its own, written after it in braces: [[bearer-tokens]] {relation: defines}. The edge holds it as e.data.

docs.title: Building a graph
docs.text:
Graph(cards) — or cards | Graph — is the graph of those cards and the links among them:

cards
| filter(c => c.name == "virginia-woolf" or c.metadata.author == "Virginia Woolf")
| Graph
| text

a-room-of-ones-own
  -> virginia-woolf
mrs-dalloway
  -> virginia-woolf
the-common-reader
  -> virginia-woolf
virginia-woolf
  -> a-room-of-ones-own
  -> mrs-dalloway
  -> the-common-reader

A graph is a value with two fields, both sets: its nodes, the cards, and its edges. The vault's whole graph is bound as graph:

{nodes: graph.nodes | size, edges: graph.edges | size}

{edges: 22, nodes: 13}

A graph can also be built from edges alone, Graph(edges), or from cards and edges together, Graph(nodes, edges). Its nodes are the cards given and every edge's endpoints:

@[[virginia-woolf]] | downlinks | Graph | text

a-room-of-ones-own
  -> virginia-woolf
mrs-dalloway
  -> virginia-woolf
the-common-reader
  -> virginia-woolf
virginia-woolf

docs.title: Growing a graph
docs.text:
expand(depth = n) starts from some cards and follows links outwards, n steps, in both directions. Every node it reaches records why it is present — which card it was reached from, and how far away:

@[[mrs-dalloway]] | expand(depth = 1) | text

club  (expanded from mrs-dalloway at depth 1)
  -> mrs-dalloway
mrs-dalloway
  -> virginia-woolf
virginia-woolf  (expanded from mrs-dalloway at depth 1)
  -> mrs-dalloway

direction = "uplinks" or "downlinks" follows links one way only. A graph of matches and their neighbours never claims that the neighbours matched: the reason travels with each node.

docs.title: A relation is an edge
docs.text:
The card frankenstein-inspires-dune declares a relation in its header:

---
title: Frankenstein inspires Dune
metadata:
  category: influence
  knowledge:
    type: Relation
    relation:
      source: frankenstein
      target: dune
---

In a graph such a card is not a node but the edge it declares, between the two cards it names:

cards | of_type(RelationCard) | Graph | text

dune  (expanded from frankenstein-inspires-dune at depth 1)
frankenstein  (expanded from frankenstein-inspires-dune at depth 1)
  -> dune

docs.title: Drawing a graph
docs.text:
A graph is written in a diagram format by the step named for it. mermaid writes a Mermaid diagram and d2 a D2 one; json writes the node-link form a graph library reads:

cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book") | Graph | mermaid

graph LR
  n0["a-room-of-ones-own"]
  n1["dune"]
  n2["frankenstein"]
  n3["leaves-of-grass"]
  n4["mrs-dalloway"]
  n5["the-common-reader"]
  n6["the-hobbit"]
  n2 --> n1

In a Markdown document — chapter 11 — a graph is written as a fenced d2 block, which documentation sites draw.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: expand grew a graph from a starting card. Chapter 8 finds the starting cards for a question in words.

docs.title: 8. Finding cards by meaning
docs.text: filter answers a question with a yes or no per card. Retrieval answers a question in words with a ranking: every card that matches, best first, each with a score. HQL has two retrievals, each an extension a program imports.

docs.title: Lexical retrieval
docs.text:
lexical matches the words of a query against the words of each card. It needs nothing built in advance:

import lexical
cards | lexical("desert spice") | take(3)

[dune (0.2928), frankenstein-inspires-dune (0.2778), frankenstein (0.2471)]

import lexical makes the extension's step available to the program. Without it, the name is not a step, and the error says which import provides it:

cards | lexical("desert spice")

name error: `lexical` is provided by the `lexical` extension: write `import lexical`
 --> <expression>:1:9
  |
1 | cards | lexical("desert spice")
  |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: A ranking holds hits
docs.text:
A ranking is a sequence of hits. A hit holds the card it retrieved, as value, and its score:

import lexical
cards
| lexical("desert spice")
| take(2)
| map(h => {card: h.value.name, score: h.score})

[{card: "dune", score: 0.2927674902397191}, {card: "frankenstein-inspires-dune", score: 0.2777641653663699}]

A score is evidence that a card is relevant to the query, not relevance itself, so every hit carries the retrieval that produced it — the model, the index, the metric, and whether the search was approximate:

import lexical
ranked = cards | lexical("desert")
{model: ranked.retrieval.model, metric: ranked.retrieval.metric, approximate: ranked.retrieval.approximate}

{approximate: false, metric: "cosine", model: "hql.hashbag.v1"}

take keeps a ranking a ranking, in the retrieval's order. Any other order is the program's own: sorting a ranking by another key makes it a plain sequence of hits.

docs.title: Retrieval, then the graph
docs.text:
A ranking is a collection of cards, so every step of the earlier chapters applies. expand grows a graph from the best hits, and the nodes it adds say they were reached, not retrieved:

import lexical
cards
| lexical("a creature and its maker")
| take(2)
| expand(depth = 1)
| text

club  (expanded from frankenstein at depth 1)
  -> dune
  -> frankenstein
  -> leaves-of-grass
dune  (expanded from frankenstein at depth 1)
frankenstein  (retrieved 0.2064)
  -> mary-shelley
  -> dune
leaves-of-grass  (expanded from walt-whitman at depth 1)
  -> walt-whitman
mary-shelley  (expanded from frankenstein at depth 1)
  -> frankenstein
walt-whitman  (retrieved 0.1261)
  -> leaves-of-grass

docs.title: Semantic retrieval
docs.text:
lexical matches spellings: a card that never uses the query's words scores nothing. semantic scores by meaning, against embeddings a language model computed ahead of time into an index the vault names in hql.toml. The tutorial vault has no index; the birds corpus in tests/fixtures/birds has one. Asked for night-hunting birds, semantic finds the owls, though no owl article contains the word "night":

import semantic
cards | semantic("night hunting birds") | take(3) | map(h => h.value.title)

["Great horned owl", "Barn owl", "Strigidae"]

The same question, by spelling:

import lexical
cards | lexical("night hunting birds") | take(3) | map(h => h.value.title)

["Mute swan", "Passeriformes", "Alcedinidae"]

The binary never loads a model: contrib/semantics/ builds the index, and hql doctor checks the chain — vault, configuration, index, model, query vectors — and names the first part that is missing.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Every collection so far ended. Chapter 9 meets one that does not.

docs.title: 9. Streams that do not end
docs.text: Every collection so far had an end: a size, a last element. A stream is a succession of values whose production need not end — a log, a feed, the natural numbers. HQL types the difference, so a program cannot ask an endless stream a question that needs its end.

docs.title: A function that yields
docs.text:
A fn whose body is a block, in braces, produces its values with yield, in the order each yield is reached. Its result type says whether production ends: Seq<T> promises an end, Stream<T> does not. These are the natural numbers:

fn naturals(from: Int) : Stream<Int> {
    yield from
    for n in naturals(from + 1) {
        yield n
    }
}
naturals(1) | take(5)

[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

for name in collection { … } runs its block once per value. A block holds yield, for and bindings, one per line, and is written only as the body of a fn.

Calling naturals(1) evaluates nothing. Its value is a recipe for the numbers, and take(5) asks for five of them and then stops asking — which is what makes an endless producer usable.

docs.title: One value at a time
docs.text:
map, filter and drop take a stream and give a stream. Each value passes through the whole pipeline before the next is produced, so only as many are made as the end of the pipeline asks for:

naturals(1)
| filter(n => n % 7 == 0)
| map(n => n * n)
| take(3)

[49, 196, 441]

docs.title: Questions that need the end
docs.text:
sum, size, sort, group and the other whole-input steps need the last value before they can answer. Over a stream there may be none, and the checker says so before anything runs:

fn naturals(from: Int) : Stream<Int> {
    yield from
    for n in naturals(from + 1) {
        yield n
    }
}
naturals(1) | sum

type error: `sum` needs a finite input, and Stream<Int> may not end; bound it first with `take(n)`, or batch it with `collect(n)`
 --> <expression>:7:15
  |
7 | naturals(1) | sum
  |               ^^^

A stream becomes finite through take(n), or is answered in pieces through collect(n), which gathers consecutive values into batches of n:

naturals(1)
| collect(3)
| map(batch => batch | sum)
| take(3)

[6, 15, 24]

emit is the inverse of collect: it passes on every member of every batch, in order. flat_map(f) is map(f) | emit.

[[1, 2], [3]] | emit

[1, 2, 3]

docs.title: A sequence over the vault
docs.text:
A generator that promises an end is a Seq. This one yields the title of each book, in title order — a sequence the vault's cards produce on demand:

fn titles() : Seq<String> {
    for c in cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book") | sort(by = c => c.title) {
        yield c.title
    }
}
titles() | take(3)

["A Room of One's Own", "Dune", "Frankenstein"]

cards itself is such a sequence: the vault's cards, produced as the walk of the folder reaches each one.

docs.title: Writing a stream
docs.text:
Formatting an endless stream writes it piece by piece as it arrives: a line of text, a JSON value per line, a CSV row. hql flushes each piece, and a reader that stops reading ends the stream:

naturals(1) | map(n => n * n) | json

$ hql eval '…naturals… | map(n => n * n) | json' | head -3
1
4
9

A diagram format describes a whole, so | mermaid over a stream is refused until take(n) bounds it.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 10 is about every format a value can be written in, and who chooses it.

docs.title: 10. Writing results out
docs.text: A program's value is computed first, and written second. How it is written is a presentation format — plain text, HQL, Markdown, JSON, YAML, CSV, or a diagram — and the format is a type, so a program that formats a value knows what kind of text it holds.

docs.title: Formats are a category of their own
docs.text:
Each format is a Format: Text, Lines, Hql, Markdown, Hmd, Json, JsonLines, Yaml, Csv, D2 and Mermaid. A format describes how values are written, not the text itself: a step named for a format encodes any value in it, and what comes out is a String:

cards | filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo") | map(c => c.title) | markdown

- Leaves of Grass
- The Common Reader
- The Hobbit

cards | filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo") | map(c => c.title) | markdown

String

A formatted value is a string that remembers its format, so a host prints it as it is. A later step may read it, and comparing it with a string compares the text:

([1, 2] | json) == "[\n  1,\n  2\n]"

true

A card written as Markdown is its body; a list of cards, a list of links:

cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "author") | markdown

- [[frank-herbert]]
- [[jrr-tolkien]]
- [[mary-shelley]]
- [[virginia-woolf]]
- [[walt-whitman]]

docs.title: The longhand, format
docs.text:
markdown is the shorthand for format(Markdown). The longhand takes two options. limit keeps the first n elements and says how many were cut:

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
| map(c => c.title)
| format(Text, limit = 3)

["A Room of One's Own", "Dune", "Frankenstein"]
… 4 more not shown

A list of records in Markdown is a bullet list. A table is a value of its own type, Table: Table(xs, columns = [...]) takes one row per record and the columns in the order written, and every format writes it as a table, a pipe table in Markdown:

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
| map(c => {title: c.title, pages: c.metadata.pages})
| Table(columns = ["title", "pages"])
| markdown

| title               | pages |
| ------------------- | ----- |
| A Room of One's Own | 112   |
| Dune                | 412   |
| Frankenstein        | 280   |
| Leaves of Grass     | 145   |
| Mrs Dalloway        | 194   |
| The Common Reader   | 304   |
| The Hobbit          | 310   |

The same table in Csv is a header row and one row per record, in Json an array of objects with their keys in column order, and in Text space-aligned columns. renderer names one of a format's encoders for a shape over the vault's choice, format(Markdown, renderer = "mermaid") for a graph; a table renderer, such as pipe, writes only a Table.

A format that cannot write a value is refused before the program runs:

1 | d2

type error: no renderer writes Int as D2
 --> <expression>:1:5
  |
1 | 1 | d2
  |     ^^

docs.title: Choosing the format from outside
docs.text:
A program that does not format its result is written as HQL — the literal you would type to get the value back, a string in quotes. --to text writes a string bare instead, and --to names any other format without changing the program:

cards | filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo") | map(c => c.title)

- Leaves of Grass
- The Common Reader
- The Hobbit

--to none evaluates the program and writes nothing. --envelope json wraps the answer for another program to read: the type, the value, and every report:

cards | filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo") | size

{
  "origin": "<expression>",
  "reports": [],
  "type": "Int",
  "value": 3
}

The order is fixed: a format step in the program wins, then --to, then the host's own — Markdown for a document, HQL for a terminal.

docs.title: A vault chooses its renderers
docs.text:
Which renderer writes a type in a format is the vault's choice, in its hql.toml, over the built-in defaults. A graph in Markdown is a D2 diagram unless the vault says otherwise:

[format.Graph]
markdown = "mermaid"

A renderer or format the binary does not have fails loading the vault, so the mistake is reported before any query runs.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: A document is where most results end up. Chapter 11 puts queries inside documents and builds the documents they describe.

docs.title: 11. Queries inside documents
docs.text: A document can hold the queries that compute parts of it. hql render runs them and builds the document they describe, so a reading list, an index or a status table is a query, not a list somebody keeps up to date.

docs.title: Cells
docs.text:
A fenced block whose info string is hql — or hql#eval, or hql#query — is a cell. This is examples/notebook/reading-list.hmd:

# The club's reading list

Built from the vault with `hql --vault examples/tutorial render`.

```hql id=books hidden
cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
```

## Still to read

```hql id=todo
books
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| sort(by = c => c.title)
| map(c => c.title)
```

## How far along

```hql
{books: books | size, to_read: todo | size}
```

docs.title: Building the document
docs.text:
hql render runs every cell against the vault and writes the document with each cell replaced by its output, as Markdown:

hql --vault examples/tutorial render examples/notebook/reading-list.hmd

# The club's reading list

Built from the vault with `hql --vault examples/tutorial render`.

## Still to read

- Leaves of Grass
- The Common Reader
- The Hobbit

## How far along

| key     | value |
| ------- | ----- |
| books   | 7     |
| to_read | 3     |

The source is the program; the built document is its result. --write <file> writes the build to a file instead of standard output.

docs.title: Cells share values
docs.text:
A cell's info string carries attributes after its kind:

  • id=<name> exports the cell's value to the other cells of the document, under that name. books and todo above are such names.
  • hidden runs the cell and writes nothing, for a value other cells read.
  • replace or after chooses where that one cell's output goes.

Only a cell's value leaves it: a binding inside a cell stays in that cell. The cells form a dependency graph, and run in the order their reads require, not the order they are written in. A cycle or a duplicate id is an error naming the cells, and a cell that reads a failed one is skipped, saying which cell it waited on.

The document is checked as a whole before any cell runs, so a type error in the last cell stops the build before the first one runs.

docs.title: Keeping the cells
docs.text:
--emit after keeps every cell and writes its output after it, between two comments a Markdown preview does not display:

```hql id=todo
books
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| sort(by = c => c.title)
| map(c => c.title)
```
<!-- hql:output id=todo hash=9c9f41e99b94 status=ok -->
- Leaves of Grass
- The Common Reader
- The Hobbit
<!-- /hql:output -->

With --in-place that rewrites the source itself, the way a notebook saves its outputs, and the next render replaces what is between the markers. The opening marker records the cell's id, a hash of its code and of the code of every cell it reads, and its status. An output whose hash differs from the cell's current one is stale, and an editor can say so without running anything.

--cell <id> runs one cell and the cells it reads, and rewrites only its output. --envelope json prints the built document and a record per cell — its id, span, hash, type, status, output and reports — for an editor to read.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 12 is about the tools around the language: the REPL, the reports, and what hql says when something is wrong.

docs.title: 12. Working with hql
docs.text: The language is half of what you use; the other half is the command and what it says back. This chapter is about the tools: the commands, the reports, and the messages hql writes when a program is wrong.

docs.title: The commands
docs.text:
Command What it does hql eval <program> check and evaluate a program given as an argument hql run <file> check and evaluate a program in a file; - reads standard input hql check <file> write the program's type, and the signature of every alias, without evaluating hql repl read, evaluate and print, keeping bindings between lines hql render <file> build a document from its cells (chapter 11) hql builtins list every step, by the provider that implements it, with its signature hql config the settings in force, and where each came from hql doctor check the semantic-search chain and name the first missing part

--vault <dir> names the vault, --to <format> the output format, and --envelope json wraps the answer for another program.

docs.title: The REPL
docs.text:
hql repl keeps its bindings from one input to the next. The arrow keys edit a line and recall earlier inputs, from a history kept between sessions. An input goes on over several lines while a bracket is open, or while the next line opens with |, so every program in this book can be pasted in as it is written. :type asks for the type of an expression, or, given a function's name, prints the standard library's declarations of it, one per overload. :quit leaves, as do quit, exit and Ctrl-D:

$ hql repl
hql 0.5.0. `:help` for commands, `:quit` to leave.
hql> shelf = [412, 280]
()
hql> shelf | sum
692
hql> :type shelf
List<Int>
hql> :type range
fn range(start: Int, end: Int, step: Int = 1) : List<Int>    // std/seq
hql> :quit

docs.title: What a step takes
docs.text:
hql builtins lists every step with its signature, one line per form:

$ hql builtins
core 0.5.0 (always available)
  size
    Collection<T> | size<T>() -> Int
    Count all element occurrences.
  contains
    Collection<T> | contains<T>(value: T (positional)) -> Bool
    Whether a value occurs in the collection.
  …

A function of a module that the program has not imported is listed too, so the import it needs can be looked up. import lexical makes a module visible; lexical.lexical(…) names a function with its module, when two visible modules declare one name and the input does not tell them apart. The modules of lib/std/prelude.hql, string, seq, math, option, result, graph, format and io among them, are visible in every program unless the vault's hql.toml says prelude = false.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
A run produces a value and a queue of reports: warnings that change nothing, errors that make a result wrong, failures that make one impossible. Every report names where it points, by line and column.

By default hql stops at the first error. --report collect reports every error it can find:

$ hql --report collect eval 'a = nosuchthing
b = alsomissing'
name error: `nosuchthing` is not bound
 --> <expression>:1:5
  |
1 | a = nosuchthing
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^

name error: `alsomissing` is not bound
 --> <expression>:2:5
  |
2 | b = alsomissing
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^

2 reports: 0 failure, 2 error, 0 warning

A misspelled step suggests the nearest one, and a retired name says what replaced it:

$ hql eval '[1, 2] | mapp(n => n)'
name error: `mapp` is not a pipeline step; did you mean `map`?

A warning never changes the exit status. Names have one casing per kind — snake_case for bindings, functions and fields, PascalCase for types — and a name off its kind's convention is a warning where it is written:

$ hql eval 'bookCount = 7
bookCount'
7
type warning: `bookCount` is a binding, written in snake_case
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | bookCount = 7
  | ^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Logging from a program
docs.text:
A program reports on itself with a logger. import logging provides one; it writes structured events to an endpoint of its choosing, apart from the result:

$ hql --vault examples/tutorial 'import logging
log = Logger(stderr, Text, name = "books")
books = cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
log | info("selected", {category: "book"})
books | size'
INFO books selected {category: "book"}
7

--log-level debug lowers every logger's threshold, and --log-level warn raises it, without changing the program.

--envelope json carries every report, whatever the level, as data.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The report mode and level come from the command line, then the vault's hql.toml, then the environment ($HQL_REPORT, $HQL_REPORT_LEVEL), then the defaults. hql config says which applies, and why:

$ hql --vault examples/tutorial config
report mode: strict (from the default)
report level: warning (from the default)
vault: examples/tutorial (14 cards)

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: So far every program read a vault or its own values. Chapter 13 reads files and standard input, and writes files and standard output.

docs.title: 13. Reading and writing data
docs.text:
The io module

This chapter covers the io module, which ships in the next release. It is part of the prelude, so a program needs no import to use it.

Every program so far read a vault, or values written into the program itself. This chapter reads files and standard input, and writes files and standard output, without leaving the language. The pipeline you write stays the same whatever the data's location.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
An endpoint says where bytes are. Constructing one performs no I/O: it opens, stats and resolves nothing.

file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")

file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")

Four endpoints are bound by the host, as vault is, and need no configuration: stdin, stdout, stderr and file(path). A relative path resolves against the directory of the program file or document that names it, and against the working directory for an expression.

What an endpoint can do is its type. Stdin is Readable, Stdout and Stderr are Writable, and File is both, and Replayable: it gives the same bytes on every read within one evaluation. Reading from an endpoint that cannot be read is refused before the program runs:

source(stdout, Json)

type error: `source` needs Readable, not Stdout
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | source(stdout, Json)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Reading with source
docs.text:
source(endpoint, Format) reads every document an endpoint holds, in a format. examples/io/sightings.jsonl holds four JSON documents, one per line:

{"species": "barn owl", "site": "meadow", "seen": "dusk"}
{"species": "wren", "site": "hedge", "seen": "morning"}
{"species": "barn owl", "site": "barn", "seen": "night"}
{"species": "kingfisher", "site": "river", "seen": "morning"}

A source is an ordinary value, and a pipeline starts from it the way it starts from cards:

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"), Json)
| filter(s => s.seen == "morning")
| map(s => s.species)

["wren", "kingfisher"]

A literal path whose extension names a format — .json, .jsonl, .yaml, .csv, .txt — implies it, so the format may be left out:

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"))
| group(by = s => s.species)
| map(g => {species: g.key, sightings: g.items | size})

{{sightings: 2, species: "barn owl"}, {sightings: 1, species: "wren"}, {sightings: 1, species: "kingfisher"}}

Each document is Data, the type of a dynamically structured value from chapter 2. A CSV row is a record of strings, keyed by the header.

docs.title: Reading as a declared record
docs.text:
A binding whose declared type names an element decodes each document as that element. A tree is read as a declared record by its shape: every field at its type. A plain record, type Sighting {…}, is closed, so a document with an entry it does not declare does not decode; a record narrowing Data, type Sighting : Data {…}, is an open view that tolerates such entries and keeps them. The same reading is written as a step, source(file(p), Json) | Sighting.

type Sighting {
    species : String
    site    : String
    seen    : String
}

sightings : Seq<Sighting> = source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"))
sightings | filter(s => s.seen == "morning") | map(s => s.species)

["wren", "kingfisher"]

A function's declared result is an expected type in the same way. A CSV cell is text, so it is read as the Int, Float or Bool its field declares; a JSON leaf keeps the type it was written with. A document that does not decode stops the evaluation with an error naming the document and the field:

counts.csv: document 2 does not decode as Tally: field `count`: "many" is not an Int

docs.title: Finite or live: the type decides
docs.text:
A file is replayable, so reading it gives a Seq: it ends, and every step in the book applies. Standard input arrives once, as it is written, so reading it gives a Stream. hql check prints each type:

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"))

Seq<Data>

source(stdin, Json)

Stream<Data>

That difference is the one chapter 9 drew. map, filter and take run over standard input one document at a time, as it arrives, and a step that needs the whole input is refused until the stream is bounded or batched. The same program works on a file and on a pipe, and the checker says which steps each one allows.

tap(endpoint, Format) reads one document at a time from any readable endpoint, a file included, holding only the current one in memory. Over a file's end, file(p).end, it follows what is appended, as tail -F does:

tap(file("app.log").end, Lines) | take(1)

waits for the next line written to app.log, and returns it.

docs.title: Writing with target and sink
docs.text:
Writing has two forms, chosen by the shape of the value.

target(endpoint, Format) writes one completed value as one document. Over a file it replaces the file, atomically:

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"))
| map(s => {species: s.species, site: s.site})
| target(file("sites.csv"))

site,species
meadow,barn owl
hedge,wren
barn,barn owl
river,kingfisher

sink(endpoint, Format) writes one document per value, as each arrives. It is how a stream is written, because a stream may never complete:

source(stdin, Json)
| filter(s => s.seen == "morning")
| map(s => s.species)
| sink(stdout, Text)

"wren"
"kingfisher"

Asking target to write a stream as one document is refused, with the two ways out:

source(stdin, Json) | target(file("all.json"))

type error: `target` writes one completed value, and Stream<Data> may not end; write it piece by piece with `sink`, or bound it with `take(n)` first
 --> <expression>:1:23
  |
1 | source(stdin, Json) | target(file("all.json"))
  |                       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Writing file(p) replaces it; writing file(p).end appends. One evaluation may replace a file once or append to it any number of times, never both.

Both steps return Unit, and a Unit result prints nothing. What each one accepts, by the shape of the values:

Seq<T> Stream<T> source from a replayable endpoint from a live endpoint target one document refused: collect(n), or take(n) sink one document per element one document per value

Batches are streams of sequences, so collect(100) | sink(stdout, Json) writes one JSON array per hundred values. The format describes the encoding, and the type describes the shape: JSON lines is not a separate format, but Json written by sink.

docs.title: Branches that write
docs.text:
A tee branch from chapter 5 may end in a sink. The branch writes its documents, and the main pipeline goes on with every value:

source(stdin, Json)
| tee archived =
    filter(e => e.level == "error")
    | sink(file("errors.jsonl").end, Json)
| map(e => e.msg)
| sink(stdout, Text)

One program reads a log as it is written, appends its errors to a file, and prints every message. There is no orchestration around the query: the query is the dataflow.

docs.title: On the command line
docs.text:
With these steps hql is a structured-data tool for the shell. A first argument that names no command is a program, so hql '<program>' means hql eval '<program>':

$ cat examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql 'source(stdin, Json) | filter(s => s.seen == "morning") | map(s => s.species)'
"wren"
"kingfisher"

--to json pretty-prints each streamed document, as jq . does, and --compact gives one line each:

$ head -2 examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql 'source(stdin, Json)' --to json --compact
{"seen":"dusk","site":"meadow","species":"barn owl"}
{"seen":"morning","site":"hedge","species":"wren"}

--from names the format of standard input once, on the command line, so the program reads stdin without naming one; a format the program names wins:

$ cat examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql --from json 'source(stdin) | map(s => s.site)'
"meadow"
"hedge"
"barn"
"river"

Converting between formats is a source and a --to:

$ hql 'source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")) | map(s => s.site)' --to yaml
- meadow
- hedge
- barn
- river

Input and output stay in the program; --to only chooses how the CLI writes the final result.

docs.title: Effects and documents
docs.text:
Constructing an endpoint is pure. source, tap, target and sink are effectful: they reach outside the program, and the host decides which of them it allows.

hql render is one such host. A document reads only files under its own directory, reads no standard input, and writes nothing outside itself. A cell that tries is refused when the document is checked, before any cell runs:

type error: a document writes nothing outside itself, so `target` and `sink` are refused here
 --> report.hmd:8:7
  |
8 | [1] | target(file("out.json"))
  |       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The same program runs under different capability policies without changing its model: a terminal may write files, and a document being rendered may not.

docs.title: Configured sources
docs.text:
A program that names a file path is tied to one machine's files. A vault can instead declare its sources in hql.toml, each under an id, and a program names only the id:

[sources.journal]
kind = "vault"
root = "journal"

[sources.counts]
kind = "csv"
path = "data/counts.csv"

journal = source("journal")
journal.cards | map(c => c.name)

source("journal") is a Vault, with its own cards; source("counts") is a Seq<Data>, a row per element, decoded as a declared record where one is expected, as above. The type comes from the configuration, so checking reads hql.toml and opens nothing. The id is a literal: source(id) with a computed id is a type error, and source("postgres://db/birds") is refused with a diagnostic saying connection details belong in configuration. An id the configuration does not declare is a name error that suggests the nearest one. The data sources examples read two vaults side by side.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Not every endpoint is bytes. Chapter 14 passes values between parts of a program through channels, and logs what a program does.

docs.title: 14. Channels and logs
docs.text:
The io and io.logging modules

This chapter covers channels from the io module and the io.logging module, both shipping in the next release.

An endpoint in chapter 13 held bytes, and a format said how they were documents. A channel holds values. A logger writes structured events about a program to any endpoint, a channel included.

docs.title: Channels
docs.text:
Channel<T>(name) is an endpoint of values of type T, held in memory for one evaluation. It keeps the values' type, so it takes no format. target writes one value to it, sink writes each value of a sequence, and source gives what it holds now:

c = Channel<Int>("nums")
1 | target(c)
[2, 3] | sink(c)
source(c)

[1, 2, 3]

Reading does not consume. Two reads give the same values:

c = Channel<Int>("n")
[1] | sink(c)
a = source(c)
b = source(c)
[size(a), size(b)]

[1, 1]

tap(c) gives only what is written after it, as a stream:

c = Channel<Int>("n")
[1] | sink(c)
t = tap(c)
[2] | sink(c)
t | take(5)

[2]

The element type is checked like any other:

c = Channel<Int>("n")
"x" | target(c)

type error: Channel<Int> holds Int, not String
 --> <expression>:2:7
  |
2 | "x" | target(c)
  |       ^^^^^^^^^

One name is one channel within a program run, or within one cell of a document. A cell of a document being rendered may write a channel, because a channel stays inside the evaluation.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
A program reports on itself through a logger, apart from its result. import logging provides one. Logger(endpoint, Format, name = …) names a producer and the destination it writes to:

import logging

log = Logger(stderr, Text, name = "club")
books = cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
log | info("selected", {books: books | size})
log | debug("not shown")
books | size

INFO club selected {books: 7}
7

The event goes to standard error and the result to standard output. A logger has five operations, one per level, ordered from least to most severe: trace, debug, info, warn and error. Each takes a message and, optionally, structured data, and is called through a pipe or directly: info(log, "x") is log | info("x").

A logger writes events at its threshold or above, Info unless level says otherwise, so the debug call above writes nothing. --log-level overrides every threshold without changing the program:

$ hql --log-level debug 'import logging
log = Logger(stderr, Text, name = "club")
log | debug("now shown")
1'
DEBUG club now shown
1

The format is the endpoint's, as for sink. In Json each event is one document with four keys:

{"data":{"title":"Dune"},"level":"Warn","logger":"club","message":"low stock"}

docs.title: Logs as values
docs.text:
A logger whose destination is a Channel<LogEvent> keeps its events as values, which the rest of the program can query. A level is a type, so it is tested with is:

import logging

events = Channel<LogEvent>("events")
log = Logger(events, name = "club", level = Debug)
log | debug("loaded")
log | warn("low stock", {title: "Dune"})
log | error("missing", {title: "Ulysses"})

source(events)
| filter(e => (e.level | is(Warn)) or (e.level | is(Error)))
| map(e => {level: e.level, message: e.message})

[{level: "Warn", message: "low stock"}, {level: "Error", message: "missing"}]

Inside a document, the host binds cell, the cell being rendered. Logger(cell.logs, name = …) writes to that cell's own channel, whose events an editor shows beside the cell's result. They are never saved into the document.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: A run of a language model is one more thing a program can do, and its record one more value. Chapter 15 builds context from a vault, runs an agent over it, and reads back everything that happened.

docs.title: 15. Agents and runs
docs.text:
The ai module

This chapter covers the ai module, which ships in the next release.

Most of the work around a language model is not the call itself. Choosing evidence, building the context, writing the prompt, giving the model tools, continuing a conversation and keeping what came back are dataflow, and HQL writes them as dataflow. Every stage is a typed value: what reached the model, what it called and what it answered are read the way a card is read.

The constructors in this chapter are pure and need no import. The steps that reach a model need import ai, which is how a program states that it may spend money and send text to a third party.

docs.title: An agent is a card
docs.text:
An agent is behaviour and configuration, written as a card. Its body is its instructions, and its agent header table configures it. This one is added to the reading-club vault as librarian.hmd:

---
title: Librarian
agent:
  model: default
  tools: [books_by]
  max_turns: 4
---
# Librarian

Answer questions about the club's shelf from the cards you are given and the
tools you have. Name the books you rely on. Say so when the shelf does not
answer the question.

Agent reads one from a card:

librarian = @[[librarian]] | Agent
librarian.tools

["books_by"]

A card is an agent only by saying it is one: Agent refuses a card with no agent table, and an unknown key in it, so a misspelt max_turn does not quietly select the default. model names a key of [ai.models] in the vault's hql.toml, never a provider, so a committed card does not fix a vendor:

[ai]
recordings = ".hql/runs"

[ai.models.default]
api = "messages"
endpoint = "https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages"
model = "claude-sonnet-5-5"
max_tokens = 1024
temperature = 0

docs.title: Context and prompt
docs.text:
Context(label) turns values into what a model reads: one item per element, each written as markdown writes it, with where it came from:

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| Context("unread")
| map(i => {label: i.label, source: i.provenance.name})

[{label: "unread", source: "leaves-of-grass"}, {label: "unread", source: "the-common-reader"}, {label: "unread", source: "the-hobbit"}]

A context is a Seq<ContextItem>, so contexts are combined with concat and narrowed with filter, like any other sequence. A ranking from chapter 8 keeps each hit's score and retrieval in its item, so cards | semantic(question) | take(10) | Context("evidence") is evidence that says how it was found.

Prompt(instructions) puts the task in front of the context. Its rendered field is the text exactly as sent:

p = cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| Context("unread")
| Prompt("Which unread book should the club start with?")

p.rendered

Which unread book should the club start with?

## unread

Source: leaves-of-grass

# Leaves of Grass

Poems by [[walt-whitman]], revised and enlarged for the rest of his life.

Source: the-common-reader

# The Common Reader

Essays by [[virginia-woolf]] on reading, written for readers rather than critics.

Source: the-hobbit

# The Hobbit

A novel by [[jrr-tolkien]]. A hobbit is talked into an adventure and comes home changed.

docs.title: Tools are functions
docs.text:
A tool is a named HQL function. Tool records its name, a description and the JSON Schema of its parameters, derived from their types:

fn books_by(author: String) : List<String> =
    cards | filter(c => c.metadata.author == author) | map(c => c.title) | List

Tool(books_by, "The titles on the shelf by one author")

Tool {name: "books_by", description: "The titles on the shelf by one author", parameters: {"properties":{"author":{"type":"string"}},"required":["author"],"type":"object"}}

A tool is pure. While the harness evaluates one for a model, every effectful step is refused, so no path through the function reaches a file, a network or another model. The tools a run is given must be exactly those the agent's card lists: the card is where a reader learns what an agent can do.

docs.title: Running an agent
docs.text:
run(agent, tools = …) executes the agent over a context or a prompt until it stops, and returns a Run. This program is pick.hql:

import ai

fn books_by(author: String) : List<String> =
    cards | filter(c => c.metadata.author == author) | map(c => c.title) | List

librarian = @[[librarian]] | Agent

pick =
    cards
    | filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
    | Context("unread")
    | Prompt("Which unread book should the club start with?")
    | run(librarian, tools = [Tool(books_by, "The titles on the shelf by one author")])

pick.result

"Start with The Common Reader. It is the only unread book by Virginia Woolf, and the club has already read A Room of One's Own and is reading Mrs Dalloway, so it completes the club's Woolf."

The answer is one field among many. The harness never collapses a run into the text the model last wrote:

pick.calls | map(c => {tool: c.tool, status: c.status, output: c.output})

[{output: "[\"A Room of One's Own\",\"Mrs Dalloway\",\"The Common Reader\"]", status: "ok", tool: "books_by"}]

turns is the conversation, stop says why it ended — end, max_tokens, max_turns or refused — and model and usage are what the provider reported, not what configuration asked for. trace puts everything that happened in one order:

pick | trace | map(e => e.kind)

["prompt", "request", "response", "tool_call", "request", "response", "stop"]

docs.title: Continuing and delegating
docs.text:
A Run never changes. ask(message) continues its conversation with the same agent and tools, and returns a new run whose parent is the first:

why = pick | ask("What did you rely on?")
why.result

"The books_by tool listed three Woolf titles, and the card for The Common Reader is the only one marked todo."

delegate(agent, task) starts a fresh conversation for another agent, given the first run's context and its result. An agent named in a card's agents: list is offered to the model as a tool of that name, so a model may delegate by itself; each child run is kept in children, and delegation stops at depth three.

remember(name) writes a run's result, or a string, as a card in the vault's [ai.memory] dir. Memory is cards: writing it is one explicit step, and reading it is a query like any other.

docs.title: Recordings: a run that answers again
docs.text:
A program that reaches a model would answer differently on every evaluation. HQL keeps each response as a recording, keyed by the SHA-256 of the request it answers, under the vault's [ai] recordings directory. --ai chooses what may happen:

Mode What it does replay the default: answers from recordings only, and never reaches a network record sends what is not recorded yet, and records it live always sends

The mode is never read from hql.toml, so spending money is always a choice made on the command line. Record once, and the same program then evaluates offline, byte for byte:

$ hql --vault . --ai record run pick.hql
"Start with The Common Reader. …"
$ hql --vault . run pick.hql
"Start with The Common Reader. …"

A request with no recording is a diagnostic, not an empty answer:

evaluation failure: no recording for this request (5e10ae23…); run with --ai record
  --> pick.hql:13:7

hql check checks the whole program, its type is Run, and no model is reached. Committed recordings make a document that calls a model as reproducible as one that does not.

docs.title: Agents inside documents
docs.text:
In a cell, this is the card the cell is written in, and the prose of the cell's section — from the nearest heading above it down to the cell — is the default instructions of every Prompt it builds. The question is written once, as prose, next to its answer:

## What should we read next?

Pick one unread book for the next meeting, and say why.

```hql#eval id=next
import ai

fn books_by(author: String) : List<String> =
    cards | filter(c => c.metadata.author == author) | map(c => c.title) | List

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| Context("unread")
| run(@[[librarian]] | Agent, tools = [Tool(books_by, "The titles on the shelf by one author")])
```

The knowledge, the prompt and the program that assembles the prompt stay visible, editable and queryable in one document. hql render replays the cell from its recording; --ai host instead leaves the request for the agent an editor is chatting with, and hql ai pending and hql ai answer complete it.

docs.title: Where to go from here
docs.text: You have met the whole language: values and data, collections and functions, questions in the style of SQL, a vault of documents, graphs, retrieval, streams, formats, documents that compute themselves, data read and written through endpoints, channels and logs, and agents whose runs are values. The reference states each part precisely, and the roadmap says what comes next.

docs.title: 2. Data types
docs.text: Every value in HQL has a type, and the checker knows it before the program runs. This chapter meets the types values are built from: the scalars Int, Float, Decimal, String and Bool, and Data, the tree JSON and YAML are made of. Each has a page of its own; this one tries them in the REPL first.

docs.title: Trying values in the REPL
docs.text:
hql repl reads one input at a time, evaluates it and prints the value. A binding is kept for the inputs after it, and :type asks for a type without evaluating anything:

$ hql repl
hql 0.5.0. `:help` for commands, `:quit` to leave.
hql> pages = 412
()
hql> pages / 3
137
hql> pages % 3
1
hql> :type pages
Int
hql> title = "Dune"
()
hql> title.upper()
"DUNE"
hql> :type title
String
hql> fmt("{} has {} pages", title, pages)
"Dune has 412 pages"
hql> :quit

412 is an Int, so / divides whole numbers and drops the remainder, and % gives the remainder. "Dune" is a String, and title.upper() calls a function of String on it. fmt writes values into text, one {} each.

The same programs run with hql eval, as every program in this book does:

pages = 412
title = "Dune"
fmt("{} has {} pages", title, pages)

"Dune has 412 pages"

docs.title: A type is checked, not guessed
docs.text:
Each operation says which types it takes. An Int and a String do not add, and the program is refused before it runs:

412 + "pages"

type error: addition requires two Int, two Float or two Decimal operands
 --> <expression>:1:7
  |
1 | 412 + "pages"
  |       ^^^^^^^

There is no implicit conversion between types, except that an Int beside a Decimal widens to one. str writes a value as text, and float turns an Int into a Float:

412.str()

"412"

hql check prints a program's type without evaluating it:

$ hql check - <<< '412 / 3'
Int

docs.title: The types, one page each
docs.text:
Type What it holds Page Int a whole number, 64 bits Int Float a binary floating-point number, written 2.5f Float Decimal an exact decimal number, written 2.50 Decimal String text String Bool true or false Bool Data a tree of records, lists and scalars Data Option<T> a T, or nothing Option

Braces write three different things — a set, a Data record and, where one is declared, a map — and sets, Data and maps tells them apart. Lists, sets and maps as collections, and the steps they share, are chapter 3.

docs.title: Bool
docs.text:
A Bool is true or false. Comparisons give one, and and, or and not combine them:

3 < 4 and not (1 > 2)

true

and and or are connectives of the language, so the right side is evaluated only when the left side does not decide the answer.

A Bool is not a number, and compares only with another Bool:

true == 1

type error: `Eq` for Bool compares with Bool, not Int
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | true == 1
  | ^^^^^^^^^

A condition must be a Bool. a given condition otherwise b chooses a value by one:

pages = 412
"long" given pages > 300 otherwise "short"

"long"

A Bool is a Scalar but not Orderable: true < false means nothing.

docs.title: Data: records and lists
docs.text: The values JSON and YAML are made of — records of named fields, lists, and scalar leaves — are one type in HQL, Data. This page does with Data what jq does with JSON: build it, read into it, reshape it, and write it back out.

docs.title: A tree of values
docs.text:
A data literal is written in braces, with a key, a colon and a value per field. Values may be scalars, lists, or other records:

{title: "Dune", author: {name: "Frank Herbert", born: 1920}, tags: ["desert", "spice"]}

{author: {born: 1920, name: "Frank Herbert"}, tags: ["desert", "spice"], title: "Dune"}

A key that is not an identifier is quoted: {"first name": "Ada"}. The record prints with its keys in order, so the same tree always prints the same way.

The colon is what makes braces a record. The empty record is {:}; {} without a colon is the empty set, as {1, 2} is a set of two. So d : Data = {:} holds an empty record, and d : Data = {} is a type error: {} is a Set<Never>, which a Set<Int> binding accepts and a Data one does not.

docs.title: Reading a field
docs.text:
A path reads into the tree, one key per step:

book = {title: "Dune", author: {name: "Frank Herbert", born: 1920}}
book.author.name

"Frank Herbert"

A key the tree does not have is not an error. The key belonged to whoever wrote the record, so nothing promised it, and reading it gives absence:

book = {title: "Dune"}
book.year

none

The type says so. Reading a key of a Data record gives an Option<Data>: a some holding a tree, or none. HQL has no null; a value that may be missing is an Option, and the program says what absence means where it matters.

year = {title: "Dune"}.year
match year {
    some(_) => "dated",
    none => "undated",
}

"undated"

docs.title: Asking what a leaf is
docs.text:
A leaf of a tree could be any scalar; the record did not say. Equality compares through that, so book.title == "Dune" is an ordinary question:

{title: "Dune"}.title == "Dune"

true

Arithmetic and ordering need to know the type. is(T) asks whether a value is a T, and a match arm with a type, some(Int n), both tests and reads it:

pages = {title: "Dune", pages: 412}.pages
match pages {
    some(Int n) => n * 2,
    _ => 0,
}

824

docs.title: Lists of records
docs.text:
A list of records is a List<Data>. map applies a function to every element, and x => x.title is a function written in place, a lambda:

books = [{title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310}, {title: "Leaves of Grass"}]
books | map(b => b.title)

["Dune", "The Hobbit", "Leaves of Grass"]

| is a pipe: the value on its left is the input of the step on its right. filter keeps the elements a predicate accepts:

books = [{title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310}, {title: "Leaves of Grass"}]
books
| filter(b => match b.pages { some(Int n) => n > 300, _ => false })
| map(b => b.title)

["Dune", "The Hobbit"]

To add up the page counts, the leaves become numbers first. somes drops the absent ones, of_type(Int) keeps the leaves that are integers and reads each as the Int it holds, and sum adds them:

books = [{title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310}, {title: "Leaves of Grass"}]
books
| map(b => b.pages)
| somes
| of_type(Int)
| sum

722

Each step is checked against the type the step before it produced. After of_type(Int) the list is a list of Int, which is what sum takes; without it the checker refuses sum over trees, before anything runs.

docs.title: Reshaping
docs.text:
A data literal can hold any expression, so map builds a new record from each old one:

books = [{title: "Dune", author: "Frank Herbert"}, {title: "Emma", author: "Jane Austen"}]
books | map(b => {book: b.title, by: b.author})

[{book: "Dune", by: "Frank Herbert"}, {book: "Emma", by: "Jane Austen"}]

merge combines two records. Every key of either is kept, and a key in both takes the value from the right:

merge({title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {pages: 896, edition: "illustrated"})

{edition: "illustrated", pages: 896, title: "Dune"}

docs.title: Writing it back out
docs.text:
A value is written in a presentation format by a step named for it. The result is text of that format — Json, Yaml, Csv, Markdown — and hql writes it as it is:

[{title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310}] | json

[
  {
    "pages": 412,
    "title": "Dune"
  },
  {
    "pages": 310,
    "title": "The Hobbit"
  }
]

{title: "Dune", pages: 412, tags: ["desert", "spice"]} | yaml

pages: 412
tags:
- desert
- spice
title: Dune

[{title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310}] | csv

pages,title
412,Dune
310,The Hobbit
