A list of records becomes a table when it is built into one. Table takes the records as rows and columns names their fields in the order the table writes them; each format then writes the table in its own syntax, here a pipe table:

[{title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310}]
| Table(columns = ["title", "pages"])
| markdown

| title      | pages |
| ---------- | ----- |
| Dune       | 412   |
| The Hobbit | 310   |

Chapter 10 is about formats in full.

A program writes its data as literals, reads it from a vault's documents, as chapter 6 does, or reads a JSON, YAML or CSV file with source, as chapter 13 does.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: How Data differs from a set and from a map, all three written in braces, is the next page. A Data list is one kind of collection. Chapter 3 meets the others — lists, sets and maps of typed values — and the steps that work on all of them.

docs.title: Decimal
docs.text:
A Decimal is an exact decimal number: an integer significand of up to 512 bits, about 154 digits, and a scale, the number of digits after the point, from 0 to 154. A number written with a decimal point is a Decimal, so arithmetic on it loses nothing to binary rounding:

0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3

true

The scale is kept for display. A sum or a difference has the larger scale of its operands, and a product the sum of their scales. Equality and order are by value, so 1.50 == 1.5 is true:

[1.50, 1.50 + 1.25, 1.50 * 1.5]

[1.50, 2.75, 2.250]

A literal keeps every digit it is written with, however many there are:

123456789012345678901234567890.123456789 + 0.000000001

123456789012345678901234567890.123456790

docs.title: Division and rounding
docs.text:
/ is exact where the quotient terminates, and otherwise rounded half to even to 100 significant digits. Division by zero is an evaluation error, as it is for an Int. round(x, places) rounds half to even to places digits after the point, and round(x) to a whole number:

[10 / 4.0, round(2 / 3.0, 4), round(2.345, 2), round(2.355, 2), round(2.5)]

[2.5, 0.6667, 2.34, 2.36, 2]

docs.title: Int, Float and Decimal
docs.text:
An Int beside a Decimal widens to one of scale 0, in arithmetic and in a comparison:

[12.50 * 3, 7 - 0.25]

[37.50, 6.75]

A Float does not mix with a Decimal: a binary float carries no exact decimal value, so the program says which conversion it means. decimal(x) reads an Int, or a Float by its shortest digits, as a Decimal; float(d) gives the nearest Float and int(d) the integer part:

1.5 + 2.0f

type error: a Decimal and a Float do not mix: write `decimal(x)` to read the Float as a Decimal, or `float(d)` to read the Decimal as a Float
 --> <expression>:1:7
  |
1 | 1.5 + 2.0f
  |       ^^^^

[decimal(0.1f) + 1.5, "12.50".to_decimal().unwrap_or(0.0)]

[1.6, 12.50]

JSON, YAML and CSV carry a Decimal without loss: a number read as a Decimal field keeps the digits it is written with, and a Decimal is written as a number with its digits and scale.

docs.title: Float
docs.text:
A Float is a 64-bit binary floating-point number, written with the suffix f: 0.5f, 6.02e23f, 2f. A number with a decimal point and no suffix is a Decimal. Arithmetic on two Float operands gives a Float:

7.0f / 2.0f

3.5

A binary fraction cannot hold most decimal fractions exactly, so a sum can be a little off:

0.1f + 0.2f

0.30000000000000004

That is why a Float is the wrong type for money; a Decimal holds an amount exactly as it is written.

An Int and a Float do not mix: 1 + 2.0f is refused, and so is a Decimal beside a Float. float and int convert, the second truncating:

[1.float() + 2.0f, 3.9f.int().float()]

[3.0, 3.0]

docs.title: Int
docs.text:
An Int is a whole number: a signed 64-bit integer. Arithmetic on two Int operands gives an Int.

2 + 3 * 4

14

* and / bind tighter than + and -. Division truncates towards zero, and % is the remainder:

[7 / 2, -7 / 2, 7 % 3]

[3, -3, 1]

An Int that leaves the 64-bit range is an error, never a wrapped value:

9223372036854775807 + 1

evaluation failure: numeric overflow
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | 9223372036854775807 + 1
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The math module adds what operators do not cover:

[2.pow(10), (-5).abs(), (-5).sign()]

[1024, 5, -1]

An Int is Orderable, so <, >, min, max and sort work on it, and it compares only with another Int. float turns it into a Float, and str into a String.

docs.title: Option: a value that may be missing
docs.text:
The reading club gives a book its rating when the book is done. A book still being read has no rating yet, so the club's notes have a field some records carry and others do not:

books = [
    {title: "Frankenstein", status: "done", rating: 5},
    {title: "Dune", status: "reading"},
    {title: "A Room of One's Own", status: "done", rating: 4},
]
books | map(b => b.rating)

[5, none, 4]

HQL has no null. A value that may be missing is an Option<T>: some(x), which holds an x, or none, which holds nothing. A present value prints as the value it holds, and an absent one as none.

docs.title: The type says so
docs.text:
Reading a field of a Data record gives an Option<Data>, whichever record it reads, because the type is known before any record is:

{title: "Dune"}.rating

Option<Data>

An Option is not the value it may hold. Adding to a rating that may be missing is refused before the program runs:

rating = {title: "Frankenstein", rating: 5}.rating
rating + 1

type error: addition requires two Int, two Float or two Decimal operands, or two values of a type implementing `Add`, not Option<Data>
 --> <expression>:2:1
  |
2 | rating + 1
  | ^^^^^^

The program says what a missing rating means, and the ways to say it follow.

docs.title: A value in place of none
docs.text:
unwrap_or(default) gives the value held, or default where there is none:

books | map(b => b.rating.unwrap_or(0))

[5, 0, 4]

There is no unwrap without a default. Every way out of an Option states what absence means.

docs.title: One answer for each case
docs.text:
match takes an Option apart. The some(r) arm binds the value held to r, the none arm covers the rest, and a match that leaves a case uncovered is refused:

books | map(b => {
    book: b.title,
    verdict: match b.rating {
        some(r) => fmt("{} stars", r),
        none => "not rated yet",
    },
})

[{book: "Frankenstein", verdict: "5 stars"}, {book: "Dune", verdict: "not rated yet"}, {book: "A Room of One's Own", verdict: "4 stars"}]

is_some and is_none ask the question as a Bool, for a filter or a given:

books | filter(b => b.rating.is_none()) | map(b => b.title)

["Dune"]

docs.title: Only the values that are there
docs.text:
somes keeps the present values of a collection of options and drops the absent ones. The club's ratings so far are the ratings of the books it has finished:

books | map(b => b.rating) | somes

[5, 4]

docs.title: Comparing with a missing value
docs.text:
Equality compares through an Option: some(5) == 5 is true, and none is equal to no value. A book with no rating is not a five-star book:

books | filter(b => b.rating == 5) | map(b => b.title)

["Frankenstein"]

docs.title: Options from other places
docs.text:
A record field is one source of options; a step that may have no answer is another. to_int reads a String as an Int, and gives none where the text is not a number:

["412", "four", "310"] | map(s => s.to_int())

[412, none, 310]

A step applied to an Option is applied to the value held. map gives the result in a some, or none where there was nothing to apply it to; filter keeps a value that passes a test; and alternative gives a second option where the first is none:

[
    "412".to_int().map(n => n / 2),
    "four".to_int().map(n => n / 2),
    "1965".to_int().filter(y => y > 1900),
    "four".to_int().alternative("0".to_int()),
]

[206, none, 1965, 0]

max over an empty list, a position past the end of a string and a link to a card nobody has written are each an Option too, and each is handled the same way.

A missing value is not a failure. A computation that can fail gives a Result, ok or err, and chapter 16 meets it.

docs.title: Sets, Data and maps
docs.text:
Three kinds of value are written in braces, or hold keys and values, and they are easy to mix up. They are different types with different jobs:

Type What it is Written Set<T> distinct values of one type, with no positions {1, 2, 3} Data a tree of named fields of any types, the shape of JSON {title: "Dune", pages: 412} Map<K, V> keys of one type, each to a value of one type Map(["dune"], [412])

docs.title: The colon tells braces apart
docs.text:
Braces holding values are a set; braces holding key: value entries are Data. The colon is the only thing that tells them apart, and the empty forms keep it: {} is the empty set and {:} the empty Data.

{3, 1, 3, 2}

{3, 1, 2}

{title: "Dune", pages: 412}

{pages: 412, title: "Dune"}

{}

{}

{:}

{:}

A set keeps each value once. A Data record prints its keys in order, so the same tree always prints the same way.

{} has a definite meaning, the empty set, so it is not an empty record:

d : Data = {}
d

type error: `d` is declared Data but its value is Set<Never>
 --> <expression>:1:12
  |
1 | d : Data = {}
  |            ^^

{} is a Set<Never>: a set with no elements, and so no element type yet. A declared set type gives it one:

seen : Set<Int> = {}
seen | size

0

docs.title: Data is not a map
docs.text:
Data is the type of values whose shape is not known to the program: what a JSON or YAML document decodes to. A record's fields may hold different types, a number beside a text beside a list, and nesting goes as deep as the document does. It is not a hash map, and not a Map<String, Any>.

A Map<K, V> is a typed mapping: every key is a K and every value a V. The constructor pairs a list of keys with a list of values:

Map(["dune", "emma"], [412, 474])

Map {"dune": 412, "emma": 474}

Map(["dune", "emma"], [412, 474]).get("dune")

412

So the three answer different needs: a set, which values; a map, which value for each key, all of one type; Data, whatever structure arrived.

docs.title: {:} is Data, or a declared map
docs.text:
{:} has no type of its own. Where nothing says otherwise it is the empty Data; where a map type is declared for it, it is that empty map:

Written Type Value {:} with nothing around it Data the empty Data record, printed {:} d : Data = {:} Data the same m : Map<String, Int> = {:} Map<String, Int> an empty map, equal to Map<String, Int>([], []) m : SortedMap<String, Int> = {:}, or OrderedMap that map type an empty map of that kind f({:}) where f takes a Map<String, Int> Map<String, Int> an empty map 
counts : Map<String, Int> = {:}
counts == Map<String, Int>([], [])

true

Data is the default, and a declared Map, OrderedMap or SortedMap turns it into that empty map. An empty literal carries no information of its own, so the type around it decides: HQL infers a type while the literal says enough, and asks for an explicit one where it does not.

This holds for the empty literal only. A non-empty keyed literal is always Data, and a declared map type refuses it:

m : Map<String, Int> = {a: 1}
m

type error: `m` is declared Map<String, Int> but its value is Data
 --> <expression>:1:24
  |
1 | m : Map<String, Int> = {a: 1}
  |                        ^^^^^^

A non-empty map is built with the constructor, Map(["a"], [1]).

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 3 uses lists, sets and maps as collections, and the steps they share.

docs.title: String
docs.text:
A String is text, written in double quotes. Its functions are called on it with a dot:

"Ada Lovelace".upper()

"ADA LOVELACE"

Its length counts characters, not bytes:

"héllo".length()

5

A position reads one character. It may be past the end, so it gives an Option<String>, printed as the character when it is present:

"Dune"[0]

"D"

+ on two strings is concatenation. Both operands are strings: "a" + 1 is a type error. fmt writes values of any type into a template, one {} each, and join puts a list of strings together with a separator:

["Dune" + " (1965)", fmt("{} has {} pages", "Dune", 412), ["a", "b", "c"].join(", ")]

["Dune (1965)", "Dune has 412 pages", "a, b, c"]

split, trim, replace_all, starts_with, contains and the rest are in the string module, visible in every program:

"  Frankenstein  ".trim().starts_with("Frank")

true

A String is Orderable, in the order of its characters, so a list of them sorts. Any value becomes text with str.

docs.title: Types, traits and modules
docs.text: The chapters so far query and transform data. This one is about the pieces a program of its own needs: records, unions, results, receiver calls, traits and modules. The Mighty Types corpus has one program per topic.

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
A type with fields is a record. Its constructor is its name, taking the fields by name or in declaration order, and a dot reads a field. A record is a type of the program that declares it, and nothing else is a Point.

type Point { x : Int, y : Int }

fn shift(p: Point, dx: Int) : Point = Point(x = p.x + dx, y = p.y)

shift(Point(x = 1, y = 2), 10)

Point(x = 11, y = 2)

A record may be generic, and takes its parameters from the values it is built from: Stack(items = [1, 2]) is a Stack<Int>. A field written email? : String is optional, reads as Option<String>, and may be left out at construction.

docs.title: Unions, and a match that covers them
docs.text:
A union lists alternatives. A match binds each member at its own type and must cover every one. The annotation on shapes holds the literal at the union, since a Circle and a Square meet nowhere on their own.

type Circle { radius : Float }
type Square { side : Float }
type Shape = union { Circle, Square }

fn area(s: Shape) : Float = match s {
    Circle c => 3.0f * c.radius * c.radius,
    Square q => q.side * q.side,
}

shapes : List<Shape> = [Circle(radius = 1.0f), Square(side = 2.0f)]

shapes | map(area)

[3.0, 4.0]

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Result<T, E> is a computation that may have failed: ok(v) or err(e). ok(p) and err(p) match one, and a match covers both. The ways out mirror Option's, unwrap_or, map_err, and_then, and there is no unwrap.

fn parse(text: String) : Result<Int, String> = match text.to_int() {
    some(n) => ok(n),
    none => err(fmt("not a number: {}", text)),
}

["4", "x"] | map(parse)

[ok(4), err("not a number: x")]

docs.title: Receiver calls
docs.text:
value.f(args) calls a function declared with a receiver, self, with the value as that receiver, resolved by the value's type among the modules in scope. The prelude's modules, string, seq, math, option and result, need no import, so text, sequences and options have their functions at hand. c.title without parentheses is still a field read.

"  Hello, World  ".trim().lower().split(", ").map(w => w.upper()).join(" / ")

"HELLO / WORLD"

string.trim(s) is the same call written with its module, and s | trim the same declaration as a pipeline step. Two modules may declare one name: "abc".contains("b") is the string's and [1, 2].contains(2) the collection's, told apart by the receiver. A function declared without self takes no receiver: range(1, 3) and 1 | range(3) call it, and 1.range(3) is refused.

docs.title: Traits and operators
docs.text:
A trait is a compile-time contract: the functions a type provides to satisfy it, some with a default body. impl Name for Type provides it once per trait and type, and the operators resolve through the core traits: + through Add, == through Eq, and a type implementing Ord sorts.

type Vec2 { x : Int, y : Int }

impl Add for Vec2 {
    fn add(self, other: Vec2) : Vec2 = Vec2(x = self.x + other.x, y = self.y + other.y)
}

Vec2(x = 1, y = 2) + Vec2(x = 3, y = 4)

Vec2(x = 4, y = 6)

Traits has a page of its own: required functions and default bodies, bounds, a trait extending a trait, and how a trait differs from class inheritance.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
import a.b makes one module visible under its last segment, b, and import a.b as c under c. A standard module is reached the same way, import io.net or import regex. A workspace module is an HQL file under a module root, named by its position: lib/mighty/geometry.hql is mighty.geometry, lib/mighty/mod.hql would be mighty. The roots come from hql.toml, [modules] roots = ["lib"], or from --modules lib on the command line.

A module declares functions, types, traits and implementations, and may import for itself:

// lib/mighty/geometry.hql
type Circle { radius : Float }
type Rect { width : Float, height : Float }

fn circle_area(c: Circle) : Float = 3.0f * c.radius * c.radius
fn rect_area(r: Rect) : Float = r.width * r.height
fn scale(r: Rect, k: Float) : Rect = Rect(width = r.width * k, height = r.height * k)

Its functions are reached as geo.f(…); the types it declares are visible by their names, since there is one lattice:

import mighty.geometry as geo

geo.rect_area(geo.scale(Rect(width = 2.0f, height = 1.5f), 2.0f))

12.0

Every module file opens with its name, checked against the file's place under its root: lib/mighty/text.hql opens with module mighty.text. A module that adds a pattern, module mighty.text for String, is a receiver module: its functions take self, and once the module is imported they resolve as value.f() for every value the pattern fits.

// lib/mighty/text.hql
module mighty.text for String

fn shout(self) : String = fmt("{}!", self.upper())
fn is_blank(self) : Bool = self.trim().length() == 0

import mighty.text

["hello world".shout(), text.shout("hi"), str(text.is_blank("   "))]

["HELLO WORLD!", "HI!", "true"]

is_blank is qualified because the prelude's string declares a receiver is_blank too: two imported declarations of one name are an ambiguity, and qualifying the call resolves it. A declaration the unit writes itself wins over every import's, in every spelling.

Every module is an import unit: its imports, and the prelude, are visible in it and nowhere else. A module is a closure: it sees no host binding, so vault, cards and stdin belong to the program alone, and what a module needs from a program reaches it as an argument. Inside a module a declaration is public unless it is marked private; a private function, type, trait or binding is visible only within its own module and is never reached by an importer, by name, as a receiver call or as a step.

Imports sit at the head of a source unit, two imports may not share a local name, and a module may not import itself through a cycle. The standard library's own modules are written the same way, as contracts in lib/std/: lib/std/string/mod.hql opens with module string for String and declares fn trim(self) : String with no body, which the binary implements.

docs.title: Traits
docs.text: A trait is a compile-time contract: a named set of functions over a type, each taking that type as self. A type satisfies a trait through one implementation, impl Trait for Type. A function of a trait is either required, a signature with no body that every implementation supplies, or has a default body, which an implementation inherits unless it writes the function itself.

docs.title: A trait and an implementation
docs.text:
Shape requires area and gives describe a default body. impl Shape for Rect writes area alone:

trait Shape {
    fn area(self) : Float
    fn describe(self) : String = fmt("area {}", self.area())
}

type Rect { width : Float, height : Float }

impl Shape for Rect {
    fn area(self) : Float = self.width * self.height
}

describe is a function of every Rect all the same, with the trait's body. The programs below run with these declarations before them:

Rect(width = 2.0f, height = 3.0f).describe()

"area 6.0"

docs.title: A default body calls the implementation
docs.text:
Inside a default body, self.area() resolves to the area of the type self has. The body is written once, against the required functions, and each type it runs over contributes its own:

type Circle { radius : Float }

impl Shape for Circle {
    fn area(self) : Float = 3.0f * self.radius * self.radius
}

[Rect(width = 2.0f, height = 3.0f).describe(), Circle(radius = 1.0f).describe()]

["area 6.0", "area 3.0"]

docs.title: Replacing a default
docs.text:
An implementation that writes a function the trait gives a default replaces the default for its type, and leaves it in place for every other type:

type Square { side : Float }

impl Shape for Square {
    fn area(self) : Float = self.side * self.side
    fn describe(self) : String = fmt("a square of side {}", self.side)
}

[Rect(width = 2.0f, height = 3.0f).describe(), Square(side = 2.0f).describe()]

["area 6.0", "a square of side 2.0"]

docs.title: What an implementation must supply
docs.text:
An implementation without one of the required functions is refused against its impl line, and the diagnostic names the function:

trait Shape {
    fn area(self) : Float
    fn describe(self) : String = fmt("area {}", self.area())
}

type Circle { radius : Float }

impl Shape for Circle {
    fn describe(self) : String = "a circle"
}

Circle(radius = 1.0f).describe()

type error: `impl Shape for Circle` lacks `area`
 --> <expression>:8:1
  |
8 | impl Shape for Circle {
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A trait has one implementation per type in a program. A second is refused:

trait Named {
    fn name(self) : String
}

type Dog { tag : String }

impl Named for Dog {
    fn name(self) : String = self.tag
}

impl Named for Dog {
    fn name(self) : String = "a dog"
}

Dog(tag = "rex").name()

type error: `Named` is already implemented for Dog, in this program, at byte 71: a trait has one implementation per type
  --> <expression>:11:1
   |
11 | impl Named for Dog {
   | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Generic functions over a trait
docs.text:
A bound, T : Shape, restricts a type parameter to the types that implement the trait. Inside the body x.area() resolves through the bound, and every call is checked against it:

type Circle { radius : Float }

impl Shape for Circle {
    fn area(self) : Float = 3.0f * self.radius * self.radius
}

fn total<T : Shape>(xs: List<T>) : Float = xs | map(x => x.area()) | sum

[total([Rect(width = 2.0f, height = 3.0f), Rect(width = 1.0f, height = 1.0f)]), total([Circle(radius = 1.0f)])]

[7.0, 3.0]

A type with no implementation is refused at the call:

trait Shape {
    fn area(self) : Float
}

type Line { length : Float }

fn total<T : Shape>(xs: List<T>) : Float = xs | map(x => x.area()) | sum

total([Line(length = 2.0f)])

type error: `total` needs T : Shape, and Line does not implement `Shape`
 --> <expression>:9:1
  |
9 | total([Line(length = 2.0f)])
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: A trait is not a type
docs.text:
A trait's name appears only where a contract is meant: in a bound, in an impl, and in another trait's declaration. It is not a type, so no parameter, binding or list is typed by one:

trait Shape {
    fn area(self) : Float
}

fn doubled(s: Shape) : Float = s.area() * 2.0f

1

name error: unknown type `Shape`
 --> <expression>:5:15
  |
5 | fn doubled(s: Shape) : Float = s.area() * 2.0f
  |               ^^^^^

A list that holds a Rect and a Circle together is typed by a union of the two, and a match reaches each member at its own type, where its implementation applies:

type Figure = union { Rect, Circle }

figures : List<Figure> = [Rect(width = 2.0f, height = 3.0f), Circle(radius = 1.0f)]

figures | map(f => match f {
    Rect r => r.describe(),
    Circle c => c.describe(),
})

["area 6.0", "area 3.0"]

A later release names that union in the trait's declaration, trait Shape as Figure, so that List<Figure> holds every implementing type and f.describe() needs no match. The current release does not parse it yet.

docs.title: A trait extending a trait
docs.text:
A trait may extend others, trait Greeter : Named. The functions of the traits it extends are its own, so its default bodies may call them, and an implementation of it supplies them:

trait Named {
    fn name(self) : String
}

trait Greeter : Named {
    fn greet(self) : String = fmt("hello, {}", self.name())
}

type Dog { tag : String }

impl Greeter for Dog {
    fn name(self) : String = self.tag
}

Dog(tag = "rex").greet()

"hello, rex"

Implementing Greeter does not implement Named. A bound T : Named takes only the types with an impl Named of their own:

trait Named {
    fn name(self) : String
}

trait Greeter : Named { }

type Dog { tag : String }

impl Greeter for Dog {
    fn name(self) : String = self.tag
}

fn names<T : Named>(xs: List<T>) : List<String> = xs | map(x => x.name())

names([Dog(tag = "rex")])

type error: `names` needs T : Named, and Dog does not implement `Named`
  --> <expression>:15:1
   |
15 | names([Dog(tag = "rex")])
   | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Operators are traits
docs.text:
The operators resolve through the core traits, which are in scope everywhere: + through Add, - through Sub, * through Mul, / through Div, % through Rem, == through Eq, xs[i] through Index and xs[a:b] through Slice. Implementing one gives a type its operator:

type Vec2 { x : Int, y : Int }

impl Add for Vec2 {
    fn add(self, other: Vec2) : Vec2 = Vec2(x = self.x + other.x, y = self.y + other.y)
}

Vec2(x = 1, y = 2) + Vec2(x = 3, y = 4)

Vec2(x = 4, y = 6)

A type implementing Ord is ordered. Its compare decides <, sort, min and max:

type Version { major : Int, minor : Int }

impl Ord for Version {
    fn compare(self, other: Version) : Ordering =

docs.title: Traits and inheritance
docs.text:
A default body is the part of class inheritance a trait has: code written once against functions each type defines. The rest is absent.

Class inheritance A trait a subclass inherits method bodies an implementation inherits default bodies a subclass inherits fields a trait declares no fields a subclass is a subtype of its parent a trait is not a type; no value is held as a Shape a method overrides along a chain of parents, reaching up with super an implementation replaces a default, one level, with no super a class extends one parent or several a trait extends traits; a type implements each trait it needs, once

Where one value is genuinely another, as a Card is a Doc, HQL says so with an ordinary : between types, not with a trait.

docs.title: A receiver function without a trait
docs.text:
A receiver module adds functions to a type with no trait at all. module counting for Int makes each self function after it a function of every Int:

module counting for Int

fn twice(self) : Int = self * 2

[3.twice(), 21.twice()]

[6, 42]

The functions reach only the source unit that declares the module or imports it. Elsewhere the call is a name error, as "hi".shout() is without import mighty.text (Modules):

"hi".shout()

name error: String has no function `shout`; did you mean `sort`?
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | "hi".shout()
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^

Two imported modules that declare one name over one type make a call by that name ambiguous, and the call is refused until it is qualified. A declaration the unit writes itself wins over every import's.

A trait is the form for a function that generic code quantifies over or an operator resolves through. A receiver module is the form for a function a type gains that nothing quantifies over.

docs.title: A module that implements a trait
docs.text:
A later release joins the two forms: a receiver module lists traits after its pattern, and its self functions are the implementation of those traits. The current release does not parse the trait list yet:

module shapes.circle for Circle : Shape

type Circle { radius : Float }

fn area(self) : Float = 3.0f * self.radius * self.radius

module shapes.circle for Circle : Shape means impl Shape for Circle with the module's functions as the body: describe comes from the trait's default, and Circle(radius = 1.0f).describe() is "area 3.0".

  • std/retrieval — Retrieval: a corpus ranked against a query.

docs.title: search/lexical
docs.text:
module lexical

Lexical retrieval: a corpus ranked by the words it shares with a query, a hashed bag of words compared by cosine. Offline, deterministic and exact; it models no meaning, so a query and a document that share no word score zero. Imported where it is used: import lexical.

  • lexical — Lexical retrieval: a corpus ranked by the words it shares with a query, a hashed bag of words compared by cosine.

docs.title: lexical
docs.text:
In search/lexical.

fn lexical<T : Doc>(self: Collection<T>, query: String) : Ranking<Card>

The cards of self ranked by the words their text shares with query, as a Ranking<Card>. The text of each, and query, is a hashed bag of its words of two or more letters or digits, lowercased, and the two are compared by cosine. A card that shares no word with query scores zero and is not a hit; the rest are in descending order of score. The retrieval names the model hql.hashbag.v1 and the metric cosine, and is not approximate.

docs.title: search/semantic
docs.text:
module semantic

Semantic retrieval: a corpus ranked against a query by vectors a language model made ahead of time, read from the index that [semantics] index in hql.toml names. The query is looked up in the index too; one the index does not hold is refused. Imported where it is used: import semantic.

  • semantic — Semantic retrieval: a corpus ranked against a query by vectors a language model made ahead of time, read from the index that [semantics] index in hql.toml names.

docs.title: semantic
docs.text:
In search/semantic.

fn semantic<T : Doc>(self: Collection<T>, query: String) : Ranking<Card>

The cards of self ranked against query by the cosine of their vectors in the vault's index, as a Ranking<Card> in descending order of score; a card scoring zero or less is not a hit. query must be in the index. A card the index holds no vector for is left out of the ranking, with a warning; one changed since the index was built is scored, with a warning that its score is stale.

docs.title: std/collections
docs.text:
module collections

The operations over the collection types core declares: membership, filtering, mapping, order, grouping, joins and reductions. Each one is callable directly or as a pipeline step, and carries the shape a planner splits it by.

  • Group — One partition of a group: its key, and the occurrences with that key in input order, as items.
  • size — The number of element occurrences in self, an Int: [1, 2, 2, 3] | size is 4, and Set([1, 2, 2]) | size is 2.
  • count — The number of element occurrences in self, as size gives it: count is the kept alias of size.
  • contains — true when value occurs in self, and false otherwise: [1, 2, 3] | contains(2) is true.
  • get — The value a map holds for key, or none when the key is missing: {"a": 1} | get("a") is 1, and {"a": 1} | get("b") is none.
  • filter — The elements for which a type test holds, each at the tested type.
  • of_type — The elements whose runtime type is type or one of its subtypes, each at that type, in an F<U>: filter(x => x | is(U)).
  • is — true when the runtime type of self is type or one of its subtypes.
  • somes — The present values of a collection of options, in an F<T>; the absent ones are dropped: [some(1), none, some(3)] | somes is [1, 3].
  • oks — The success values of a collection of results, in an F<T>; the failures are dropped: [ok(1), err("x"), ok(3)] | oks is [1, 3].
  • errs — The error values of a collection of results, in an F<E>; the successes are dropped: [ok(1), err("x"), ok(3)] | errs is ["x"].
  • map — Each element through by, in a collection of the input's constructor: [1, 2, 3] | map(x => x * 10) is [10, 20, 30].
  • retry — Each element through the fallible operation, invoked again while it fails with an error when accepts (every error, without when) and fewer than attempts invocations have run.
  • take — The first n elements.
  • drop — The elements after the first n, in the input's order and type: [5, 3, 4] | drop(1) is [3, 4].
  • collect — Consecutive elements in batches of n, in order; the last batch may be shorter: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] | collect(2) is [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]].
  • emit — Every member of every sequence, in order, the inverse of collect: [[1, 2], [3]] | emit is [1, 2, 3].
  • flat_map — Each element through by to a sequence, and the members of those sequences in order: map(by) | emit.
  • sort — The elements in ascending order: by their own value order, by the key by gives each, or by a comparison by of two elements.
  • group — The occurrences partitioned by the key by gives each, as a set of Groups, each a key and its occurrences in input order.
  • join — The pairs of an element of the input and an element of other that match, each built by into, ordered by the input element's position, then other's.
  • left_join — A join that keeps every element of the input: one with no match in other is built by into with none on the right.
  • right_join — A join that keeps every element of other: one with no match in the input is built by into with none on the left.
  • full_join — A join that keeps every element of both sides, with none for the missing side; the unmatched elements of other come after the matched results.
  • cross_join — Every pair of an element of the input and an element of other, built by into, in order, with no condition: [1, 2] | cross_join(["a", "b"], into = (x, y) => [x, y]) is [[1, "a"], [1, "b"], [2, "a"], [2, "b"]].
  • semi_join — The elements of the input that match some element of other, by keys, a predicate on, or both; each is kept at most once, in its position.
  • anti_join — The elements of the input that match no element of other, by keys, a predicate on, or both, in their positions.
  • reduce — The elements folded from the left by by, from initial, or without it from the first element, the result then none over []: [1, 2, 3] | reduce(0, (a, x) => a + x) is 6.
  • sum — The sum of the occurrences, reduce(0, +); [] | sum is 0.
  • product — The product of the occurrences, reduce(1, *); [] | product is 1.
  • average — The mean of the occurrences, or none over []: [1, 2] | average is 1.5.
  • merge_all — Every map merged in order, a later key winning: reduce({:}, merge).
  • union_all — Every member of every set: reduce(Set([]), union).
  • concat_all — Every member of every sequence, in order: reduce([], concat).
  • min — The least occurrence by value order, reduce(min), or none over [].
  • max — The greatest occurrence by value order, reduce(max), or none over [].
  • variance — The population variance of the occurrences, as a Float, or none over []: [1, 2, 3, 4] | variance is 1.25.
  • count_by — The number of occurrences with each key by gives, as a map from key to count; empty over [].
  • histogram — The number of occurrences in each bucket of width, keyed by the bucket's lower bound, the greatest multiple of width not above the value, in key order: [1, 5, 12, -3] | histogram(5) is SortedMap {-5: 1, 0: 1, 5: 1, 10: 1}.
  • top_k — The k greatest occurrences, by value order or by the key by gives, greatest first, equal keys in input order: [3, 1, 4, 1, 5] | top_k(2) is [5, 4].
  • approx_distinct — An estimate of the number of distinct occurrences, size(Set(xs)); 0 over [].

docs.title: std/core
docs.text:
module core

The types every other module is written in: the scalars, the collection types, the open tree Data, absence, failure, value order, the format category and the core traits. A type sits here when a module below it would otherwise import a module above it: Data is a tree of sequences and maps, so the collection types are core types, and the operations over them are the collections module's.

  • Orderable — A type whose values have a total order: of any two values of the type, one comes first or the two are equal.
  • Scalar — A leaf: a value with no parts of its own.
  • Bool — The truth values true and false: a Scalar with equality and no order.
  • Int — A 64-bit whole number, ordered by value: 7 / 2 is 3, and 7 % 2 is 1.
  • Float — A 64-bit binary floating-point number, written with the suffix f (2.5f), ordered by value.
  • Decimal — An exact decimal number, written with a decimal point and no suffix (2.50), ordered by value: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is true.
  • String — Text, ordered character by character: "ab" + "cd" is "abcd", and "hello"[1] is "e".
  • Date — A calendar date, ordered by time.
  • Iterable — A value whose elements can each be visited: the bound an operation states when it only visits each value.
  • Collection — A finite multiset of occurrences, unordered, with no runtime representation.
  • Stream — An ordered, possibly unending run of values x0, x1, x2, ....
  • Seq — A finite stream: a collection in which every occurrence has exactly one position in 0 .. size(c) - 1.
  • List — A sequence of materialized occurrences; repeated traversal preserves positions.
  • Set — Materialized distinct values under HQL equality: count(s, x) <= 1.
  • Map — Materialized associations from distinct keys of K to values of V; not a Collection.
  • OrderedMap — A Map whose keys keep their construction positions: its keys are a Seq<K>.
  • SortedMap — An OrderedMap whose key positions follow the intrinsic total order of K.
  • Data — An open tree whose keys belong to whoever wrote them: what a YAML or JSON document is.
  • TypeContract — The supertype of a closed contract: a structural type declared type C : TypeContract = {…} has exactly its declared fields, and is validated as a contract.
  • DataContract — The supertype of an open contract: a structural type declared type D : DataContract = {…} is a view over Data with at least its declared fields, and is validated as a contract.
  • Option — An optional value of T: present, holding one T, or absent.
  • Result — A computation that may have failed: ok(value) with a T, or err(error) with an E.
  • Ordering — The result of compare(a, b): Less, Equal or Greater.
  • Type — A type written as an argument: is(Card), of_type(Card).
  • Format — The category of formats: how bytes are documents.
  • Is — What a predicate that tests its parameter's type, x => x | is(U), gives: a Bool that, where true, holds the parameter at U.
  • Eq — Equality: a == b and a != b over a type implementing Eq call its eq.
  • Ord — Order: a < b and the other comparisons over a type implementing Ord call its compare.
  • Add — Addition: a + b over a type implementing Add is a.add(b).
  • Sub — Subtraction: a - b over a type implementing Sub is a.sub(b).
  • Mul — Multiplication: a * b over a type implementing Mul is a.mul(b).
  • Div — Division: a / b over a type implementing Div is a.div(b).
  • Rem — Remainder: a % b over a type implementing Rem is a.rem(b).
  • Range — A window of positions, what a slice takes: xs[a:b] is xs[Range(start = a, end = b)], and a bound left out is absent.
  • Index — A position: xs[i] over a type implementing Index is xs.at(i), the element there or its absence.
  • Slice — A part: xs[a:b] over a type implementing Slice is xs.slice(Range(start = a, end = b)), a value of the type itself.
  • Validator — A check a value passes: a trait extending Validator is a validator type.
  • Operation — A function from I to O that also carries its shape: what an executor may assume about splitting the step.
  • Elementwise — An Operation whose result for each element depends on that element alone, so it may run over any split of its input: map and filter are elementwise.
  • Partition — An Operation that regroups its input by a key, each group running independently and completing in any order: group is one.
  • Reduction — An Operation that collapses its whole input to one value through a combiner the runtime holds, so each split may be reduced and the results combined: size combines by addition, contains by disjunction.
  • Barrier — An Operation that needs its whole input before any output, so it is not split: sort, take and reduce are barriers.
  • Pair — Two values held together, each at its own type: what zip, enumerate, entries and join produce, and what Pair(first = a, second = b) builds.
  • Violation — One reason a value does not read as a contract, as validate(T) reports it.
  • Invalid — A value that did not read as a contract, and every reason why: its contract, the value, and the violations.

docs.title: std/format
docs.text:
module format

The formats, how bytes are read as values and how values are written as text, and the codec contracts over them.

A format is a type narrowing Format, the category core declares. It names an external representation and, where it applies, its framing: Lines is text framed one record per line, JsonLines one JSON document per line. A format is not the text it encodes, so none narrows String, and it is not Format<T>, since one format encodes many value structures. Whether what is read ends is a property of the source, not of the format: source(file(p), Lines) is a Seq<String> and source(stdin, Lines) a Stream<String>.

A String is always UTF-8. Every format that holds text reads and writes UTF-8, and decoding bytes that are not UTF-8 is a decoding error.

  • Text — The plain-text format: read, the whole input is one String; written, a value is its display text, and a String its characters as they are.
  • Lines — The format of text framed one record per line: read, each line is one String; written, each element of a collection is one line: [1, 2] | lines is "1 2".
  • Hql — The format of HQL's own value notation: {a: 1, b: [true]} | hql is "{a: 1, b: [true]}".
  • Markdown — The Markdown format: read, the whole input is one String; written, a collection is a list, one item per element: [1, 2] | markdown is "- 1 - 2".
  • Hmd — The HyperMarkDown format, a narrowing of Markdown: every HyperMarkDown text is Markdown, and a value is written in it as in Markdown.
  • Json — The JSON format: read, each document is one Data value; written, a value is one indented JSON document.

docs.title: std/io
docs.text:
module io

Input and output: endpoints, the data sources read from them, and the data targets written to them. An endpoint names where bytes are and performs no I/O; a format type (module format) states how the bytes are documents; a source or target joins the two, and Seq and Stream state whether the documents end.

  • Endpoint — The abstract type of every endpoint: where bytes are.
  • Readable — An endpoint bytes can be read from, by source and tap.
  • Replayable — A Readable endpoint that gives the same bytes on every read in one evaluation, so source reads what it holds as a Seq.
  • Writable — An endpoint bytes can be written to, by target and sink.
  • Stdin — The program's standard input, bound as stdin: read once, as it arrives.
  • Stdout — The program's standard output, bound as stdout: written while the program runs, before the host presents its result.
  • Stderr — The program's standard error, bound as stderr: where diagnostics go, apart from the result.
  • FileEnd — The end of a file, after what it holds, as file(path).end: a write there appends, and tap follows what is written next, as tail -f does.
  • File — A local file, the whole of it: read, every document it holds; written, it is replaced.
  • Channel — An endpoint of values rather than bytes, held in memory for one execution scope: a program run, or one cell.
  • DataSource — What a program reads: a configured source by id, or an endpoint read in a format.
  • FiniteSource — A source of every document, in order, that ends: read from a Replayable endpoint.
  • LiveSource — A source of each document as it arrives, with no replay: read from a live endpoint.
  • KeyedSource — A finite source whose contents are addressable by a key of type K.
  • Position — A message's place in its log, ordered as the log is.
  • Message — One element of a stream with where and when it sits in it: its value, its position, an optional key and time, and its headers.
  • StreamSource — A log: Message<T>s in order, replayable within its retention.
  • Catalog — An endpoint that contains sources of type S: a database of tables, a cluster of topics.
  • VaultSource — A vault as a source: an endpoint that holds its cards, as a catalog holds tables, with its members as fields rather than names.
  • DataTarget — What a program writes to: an endpoint written in a format, or a configured target by its id.
  • file — The File at path.
  • source — Every document read from endpoint in format, decoded to T: a Seq from a Replayable endpoint, a Stream from a live one.
  • tap — The documents read from endpoint in format, one held at a time, as a Stream<T>.
  • target — Writes value as one document to endpoint in format, or to the target configured under id, and gives Unit.
  • sink — Writes each of values to endpoint in format, one document per value, and gives Unit: [{a: 1}, {a: 2}] | sink(stdout, Json) writes {"a":1} and {"a":2} on two lines.

module io.logging

Logging: structured events written to a destination, apart from the result. A logger owns no writer: it names a producer and holds a destination, as sink would write it (module io): stderr or a file in a format, a network endpoint, or a Channel<LogEvent> that keeps the events as values for the host. A program imports the module: import logging.

  • LogLevel — How severe an event is.
  • Trace — The least severe LogLevel, below Debug.
  • Debug — The LogLevel above Trace and below Info.
  • Info — The LogLevel above Debug and below Warn; a logger's threshold unless written.
  • Warn — The LogLevel above Info and below Error.
  • Error — The most severe LogLevel, above Warn.
  • LogEvent — One logged event: its level, the logger that produced it, its message and its data.
  • Logger — A producer of events: its name and the least severe level it writes.
  • trace — Writes one Trace event with message and data to log's destination when log's threshold is Trace, and gives Unit.
  • debug — Writes one Debug event with message and data to log's destination when log's threshold is at most Debug, and gives Unit.
  • info — Writes one Info event with message and data to log's destination when log's threshold is at most Info, and gives Unit.
  • warn — Writes one Warn event with message and data to log's destination when log's threshold is at most Warn, and gives Unit.
  • error — Writes one Error event with message and data to log's destination, whatever log's threshold, and gives Unit.
  • Cell — The cell hql render is running, bound as cell.

Network endpoints: transports, read and written by source, tap, target and sink like any other endpoint (module io). Constructing one sends nothing: the request a program describes happens when a source, tap, target or sink uses it, and only if the host grants the network to that program.   • WebSocket — A WebSocket connection to url: each message is a document, read as it arrives and written as it is sent.
  • Socket — A TCP connection to host on port.
  • http — The HTTP resource at url, as an Http endpoint: method is the request a write sends, "GET" unless given, and headers a map of header names to values sent with every request.
  • websocket — The WebSocket at url, as a WebSocket endpoint.
  • socket — The TCP endpoint host on port, as a Socket.

module math

Numbers, in the prelude. abs, pow and sign take an Int or a Float, and abs and sign a Decimal too; round takes a Float or a Decimal, and the rest take a Float. float, int and decimal convert between the three, since no number widens on its own except an Int beside a Decimal.

  • abs — self without its sign, at its own type: abs(-3) is 3, and abs(-1.50) is 1.50.
  • pow — self raised to exponent, both of one type: pow(2, 10) is 1024.
  • sign — -1, 0 or 1 by the sign of self, as an Int: sign(-0.5) is -1.
  • float — self as a Float, the Float nearest it: float(1.10) is 1.1.
  • int — The integer part of self, as an Int, the fraction dropped toward zero: int(-2.9f) is -2.
  • decimal — self as a Decimal: an Int exactly, and a Float by the shortest digits that read back as it: decimal(0.1f) is 0.1.
  • gcd — The greatest common divisor of self and other, at least 0: gcd(12, 18) is 6, and gcd(0, 0) is 0.
  • sqrt — The square root of self: sqrt(2.0f) is 1.4142135623730951.
  • floor — The greatest whole number not above self, as a Float: floor(-1.5f) is -2.0.
  • ceil — The least whole number not below self, as a Float: ceil(-1.5f) is -1.0.
  • round — The whole number nearest self, as a Float; a value halfway between two rounds away from zero: 2.5f | round is 3.0.
  • exp — e raised to self: exp(1.0f) is 2.718281828459045.
  • ln — The natural logarithm of self: ln(1.0f) is 0.0.
  • log10 — The base-10 logarithm of self: log10(1000.0f) is 3.0.
  • sin — The sine of self, an angle in radians: sin(0.0f) is 0.0.
  • cos — The cosine of self, an angle in radians: cos(0.0f) is 1.0.
  • tan — The tangent of self, an angle in radians: tan(0.0f) is 0.0.

module regex

Text matched against a regular expression. A pattern is a String; one that does not parse is an evaluation error at the call. The module is imported where it is used: import regex.

  • is_match — Whether pattern matches somewhere in text: "a1b22c" | regex.is_match("[0-9]+") is true.
  • find — The first match of pattern in text, or none: "a1b22c" | regex.find("[0-9]+") is "1".
  • find_all — Every non-overlapping match of pattern in text, in order: "a1b22c" | regex.find_all("[0-9]+") is ["1", "22"].
  • captures — The first match of pattern in text and its groups, whole match first, or none; a group that took no part in the match is "": "a" | regex.captures("(a)|(b)") is ["a", "a", ""].
  • replace_all — text with every match of pattern replaced by replacement, in which $1 is the first group: "a1b22c" | regex.replace_all("([0-9]+)", "<$1>") is "a<1>b<22>c".
  • replace_first — text with the first match of pattern replaced by replacement, in which $1 is the first group: "a1b22c" | regex.replace_first("[0-9]+", "#") is "a#b22c".
  • split — The pieces of text between matches of pattern, in order: "a1b22c" | regex.split("[0-9]+") is ["a", "b", "c"].

docs.text:
module seq for Seq<T>

The sequence, set and map operations beyond the core's membership, order and lookup, in the prelude. A receiver module over Seq<T>, with T bound per call; a function that takes any collection writes its receiver, self: Collection<T>, and the functions over sets and maps take theirs as a typed first parameter. A receiver S : Seq<T> comes back at its own type, and F<_> : Seq<_> rebuilt in its own constructor.

  • first — The element at position 0, or none over an empty sequence: [3, 1, 2] | first is 3.
  • last — The element at the last position, or none over an empty sequence: [3, 1, 2] | last is 2.
  • reverse — The elements of self in the opposite order, in its own constructor: [1, 2, 3] | reverse is [3, 2, 1].
  • distinct — Each value of self once, at its first position, at the type of self: [1, 2, 1, 3, 2] | distinct is [1, 2, 3].
  • zip — Pairs of the elements of self and other at equal positions, as long as the shorter: [1, 2, 3] | zip(["a", "b"]) is [Pair(first = 1, second = "a"), Pair(first = 2, second = "b")].
  • enumerate — Each element of self paired with its position, counting from 0: ["a", "b"] | enumerate is [Pair(first = 0, second = "a"), Pair(first = 1, second = "b")].
  • any — Whether by holds of some value of self; false over an empty collection: [1, 2, 3] | any(x => x > 2) is true.

docs.title: std/string
docs.text:
module string for String

The functions of a String, in the prelude. A receiver module: each function takes self, so s.trim(), string.trim(s) and s | trim are one declaration. A String is a sequence of Unicode scalar values held as UTF-8, whatever encoding its text was read from. Positions and size count code points.

  • str — The text self prints as, for a value of any type: str(some(2)) is "2".
  • fmt — The template self with each {} replaced by the text of the next of args, in order: fmt("{} of {}", 1, some(2)) is "1 of 2".
  • length — How many characters self has, counting code points: "héllo" | length is 5.
  • size — How many characters self has, counting code points; the same as length: "héllo" | size is 5.
  • upper — self in upper case: "Straße" | upper is "STRASSE".
  • lower — self in lower case: "ÀB" | lower is "àb".
  • trim — self without leading and trailing whitespace: " a b " | trim is "a b".
  • trim_start — self without leading whitespace: " a " | trim_start is "a ".
  • trim_end — self without trailing whitespace: " a " | trim_end is " a".
  • capitalize — self with its first character in upper case: "élan" | capitalize is "Élan".
  • split — The pieces of self between occurrences of separator, in order: "a,b,,c" | split(",") is ["a", "b", "", "c"].
  • join — The texts of self in order, with separator between each two: ["a", "b"].join(", ") is "a, b".
  • replace_all — self with every occurrence of from replaced by to: "aaa" | replace_all("a", "b") is "bbb".
  • replace_first — self with the first occurrence of from replaced by to: "aaa" | replace_first("a", "b") is "baa".
  • starts_with — Whether self begins with part: "hello" | starts_with("he") is true.
  • ends_with — Whether self ends with part: "hello" | ends_with("lo") is true.
  • contains — Whether part occurs in self: "hello" | contains("ell") is true.
  • index_of — The position of the first occurrence of part in self, counting characters from 0, or none: "héllo" | index_of("l") is 2.
  • last_index_of — The position of the last occurrence of part in self, counting characters from 0, or none: "héllo" | last_index_of("l") is 3.
  • occurrences — How many non-overlapping times part occurs in self; 0 for an empty part: "aaaa" | occurrences("aa") is 2.
  • strip_prefix — self without part at its start, or none when it does not begin with it: "x.hql" | strip_prefix("x.") is "hql".
  • strip_suffix — self without part at its end, or none when it does not end with it: "x.hql" | strip_suffix(".hql") is "x".
  • trim_prefix — self without part at its start, or self as it is when it does not begin with it: "x" | trim_prefix("y") is "x".
  • trim_suffix — self without part at its end, or self as it is when it does not end with it: "x.hql" | trim_suffix(".hql") is "x".
  • equals_ignore_case — Whether self and other are equal in lower case: "ABC" | equals_ignore_case("abc") is true.
  • chars — Each character of self as its own text, in order: "héy" | chars is ["h", "é", "y"].
  • lines — The lines of self, without their line breaks; a final line break opens no empty line: string.lines("a\nb\n") is ["a", "b"].
  • words — The whitespace-separated words of self: " a b\tc " | words is ["a", "b", "c"].
  • reverse — The characters of self in the opposite order: "héllo" | reverse is "olléh".
  • repeat — self written times times in a row; "" for times below 1: "ab" | repeat(3) is "ababab".
  • pad_left — self preceded by fill, repeated, until it is width characters long; a longer self as it is: "7" | pad_left(3, "0") is "007".
  • pad_right — self followed by fill, repeated, until it is width characters long; a longer self as it is: "7" | pad_right(3, "0") is "700".
  • center — self between fills until it is width characters long; an odd fill character goes after it: "ab" | center(5, "*") is "*ab**".
  • truncate — At most the first width characters of self: "hello" | truncate(3) is "hel".
  • slice — The characters of self from start up to, not including, end, counting from 0; s[start:end].
  • char_at — The character of self at position, counting from 0, or none outside the text: "hello" | char_at(1) is "e".
  • to_int — The integer self writes, surrounding whitespace aside, or none when it writes none: "-42" | to_int is -42, and "1.5" | to_int is none.
  • to_float — The number self writes, as a Float, or none when it writes none: "1e3" | to_float is 1000.0.
  • to_decimal — The exact decimal number self writes, at its written scale, or none when it writes none: "2.50" | to_decimal is 2.50.
  • to_bool — The truth value self writes as true or false, or none for any other text: "True" | to_bool is none.
  • is_empty — Whether self has no characters: "" | is_empty is true.
  • is_blank — Whether self has no characters other than whitespace: " " | is_blank is true.
  • ord — The Unicode code point of the one-character text self, or none for any other text: "a" | ord is 97.
  • chr — The one-character text of the Unicode code point self, or none for an Int that is none: 97 | chr is "a".
  • bytes — The UTF-8 encoding of self, one Int per byte: "é" | bytes is [195, 169].

module validators

Validators: the standard validator types, imported where they are used, import validators, and never by the prelude, so a program's own Email is its own. A field declared with one, email: Email, is of the one type that implements it; NonEmpty, implemented for more than one type, is named in a rule, validate tags with NonEmpty, where the field's type selects the implementation. A broken one is the violation Contract.f of kind rule.

  • Email — An email address: one @ with text before it, and a domain after it holding a . that neither opens nor closes it.
  • NonEmpty — Text that is more than whitespace, or a list with an element.

docs.title: Implementations
docs.text:
impl Email for String

A String is an Email when it holds exactly one @, does not open with it, and the text after it contains a . and neither opens nor closes with one.

impl NonEmpty for String

A String is NonEmpty when it is not empty once trimmed of whitespace.

impl<T> NonEmpty for List<T>

A List is NonEmpty when it has at least one element.

module vault

The current vault: the source a program runs against. A host with a vault binds it as vault in the program module; a program running without one has no vault binding, and no module sees it.
